subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-STATEMENT AS TO DISMISSAL

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-STATEMENT AS TO DISMISSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I wish to make a statement with respect to the case of George Victor Spencer.
When this case was disclosed to the public in May, 1965, there was clear evidence in the hands of the government which established that the Soviet officials in question had engaged in activities incompatible with their official status and that their continued presence here was contrary to our national interest. As explained by the Prime Minister at that time, the matter was publicized in order to impress upon Canadians the need for constant vigilance when faced with approaches by foreign officials or agents. The issue of
declaring the Soviet officials persona non grata is quite separate from any question as to what could or should be done in respect to any person who assisted them in Canada.
At the time of the original disclosure the Prime Minister stated that consideration was being given to determine whether charges against Spencer should be laid. The evidence was referred to the law officers of the Department of Justice, who were of the opinion that much of the evidence could not meet the requirements of the rules of evidence in criminal cases. Consequently they recommended against instituting criminal proceedings.
I agreed with this advice and, as Attorney General, saw no purpose to be served in commencing proceedings which not only had no reasonable prospect of success, but would also have resulted in the disclosure, even in in camera proceedings, of counterespionage methods, the secrecy of which is so important to national security. Nevertheless the evidence was of such a nature that it could not be ignored by the government, and some action had to be taken in the case.
It should be borne in mind that in security investigations the primary objectives are always the immediate removal of the security threat, and to ascertain the nature and extent of the information which the suspect has already supplied. Although the possibility of prosecution is not lost sight of throughout these investigations, the achievement of the primary objective may produce evidence which is not admissible under the rules of evidence applicable in our courts. The present case falls into this category.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
As to surveillance, I said, in the course of a television program, that there would be surveillance on this man as long as he remains in Canada. It would be irresponsible not to keep such a man under surveillance fitted to the needs of the case. As already mentioned, security operations are primarily preventive in nature and success must often depend on surveillance. It is for preventive reasons that surveillance, to the extent necessary, will continue in this case.
On this matter of surveillance I wish to add these general remarks. There is nothing
426	COMMONS
Administration of Justice in the law to prevent the reasonable surveillance of persons for the purpose of detecting and preventing the commission of criminal offences. This does not relate only to criminal activity respecting security, but is true of criminal activity generally. To suggest there is anything unlawful or improper in members of police forces undertaking surveillance is to ignore the indisputable fact that reasonable surveillance is essential to law enforcement and is carried out by police forces everywhere in and out of Canada.
The government was not responsible for the public identification of this man. On the contrary, every reasonable precaution was taken to protect his identity. His public identification was brought about by his own behaviour in relation to the press. As for naming the man on a television program, I would point out that the program in question took place on November 28, 1965, which was more than three weeks after he had already been identified publicly by his full name as reported in the press.
As to the circumstances under which this man's name became public knowledge, let me refer you to the transcript of a portion of the television program which preceded my appearance. A Vancouver reporter was described as the man who "broke the story". He was said to have been invited to have coffee with a "mysterious stranger whom he deduced to be the missing spy". This reporter described how he visited the man's home and went on to identify Spencer by name. He also said, and I quote, "he" this is a reference to Spencer "did make certain admissions. He said he was indeed the man accused by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He said that he certainly knew something about the world of international espionage".
I also wish to confirm to the house that which was made public by my colleague the Postmaster General on December 30. I refer to Spencer's dismissal from the public service by the Governor in Council under authority of section 50 of the Civil Service Act. It is said, and correctly, that by invoking section 50 Spencer was deprived of the right of appeal to the Civil Service Commission which he might otherwise have had. This decision was made for reasons of public policy.
I wish to state, however, that in order to ensure that a final decision whether to dismiss Mr. Spencer might be arrived at on the basis of independent and objective advice, the Civil Service Commission was asked to make a full examination of the case from the point

DEBATES	January 31, 1966
of view of employment and to provide its advice. The commission advised the Postmaster General that this was a proper case for removal under the provisions of section 50 of the Civil Service Act, and this advice was accepted.
I want to emphasize that the investigation in this case was handled in the same way as other security investigations were handled prior to the time this government took office in 1963. If this case proves anything, it proves the effectiveness of Royal Canadian Mounted Police counterintelligence. I am satisfied that our security operations are in good hands, and I have seen nothing to suggest there are valid grounds for objecting to the manner in which these operations are being conducted.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-STATEMENT AS TO DISMISSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the concluding remarks of the minister are concerned, I think there will be general agreement. I have known the activities of the mounted police from the days before they had the descriptive word "royal" placed in front of their name. I know of their activities in connection with counterespionage, and I agree that what they have done generally has been in keeping with the security of the state.
I would, however, like to add one word, not by way of criticism; but I believe the commissioner of the mounted police should not be getting into print as often as he does by the observations that he makes. Recently he criticized the Globe and Mail of Toronto for an allegation that was made in that paper in which the Minister of Justice allegedly had had a conversation with the commissioner. He rushed into print, wrote a letter and stated there was no truth in it, and it turned out in the letter he wrote that the source of his information was the Minister of Justice himself. Well, the source of the information for the Globe and Mail was the Minister of Justice himself. The minister says that is not so, that he was not the source of this information, but that is what the commissioner said in his letter to the press, which bears out the advisability of the head of the mounted police not rushing into print.
Now I come to a discussion of the general purport of the statement just made. First of all, I would think that when statements of this kind are to be made the courtesy of notice should be given, whether or not this has been done in the past, so we can have our files before us. The minister apparently failed to recall that it was a press statement issued in great detail which started the discussion of
January 31, 1966

this matter, a statement giving an amount of detail which should not have been given unless there was foundation for it, and available evidence. It was stated that Spencer had received thousands of dollars, as I recall the press statement, and that he had not assisted the police in the investigation. One alleged wrongdoer had furnished information and assistance, but this man had not. This statement also said that he was compromising female civil servants in order to get the kind of information he was endeavouring to procure.
The only reason for non-prosecution which was given then was that this man was seriously ill, suffering from cancer. That was the only reason. Later on Spencer said the government was afraid to go ahead against him because he would reveal some things which were disturbing. That was the purport of the general remarks he made.
I do not think this matter can be glossed over as simply as was attempted by the Minister of Justice. I have no sympathy of any kind with this type of wrongdoing, but simply to brush the whole thing aside and say there is not sufficient evidence on which to convict is, to my mind, altogether unsatisfactory, bearing in mind the fact that the press had set forth in detail whatever evidence was available and that the Prime Minister had given as his reason for nonprosecution the dangerous illness of this man.
Now the government say "We do not want to reveal these matters because certain information of security importance would become public and we do not want that to happen; and anyway, we have no case." Naturally I do not wish to see anything revealed which would in any way weaken the counterespionage activities of our country. At the same time, there are other means. I think there should be a committee of judges-two or three judges, we will say, of the Supreme Court of Canada-to look into this without publicity being given to it. Always in history, when there has been any desire to do that which is unacceptable, the answer of those doing it has invariably been that what is being done is in the public interest.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
I think this man, regardless of his identity and actions, is entitled to a hearing. Even more so, the Canadian people are entitled to this. The attitude taken by the Minister of Justice is that he has no case; "we have no case but we are going to follow this man wherever he goes". That surely is an unusual position. The excuse given is that always, when there is an endeavour to ascertain 23033-28J
Administration of Justice whether wrongdoing is about to take place, action along that line is taken. That is true. But to continue a course of surveillance of this kind, continuing surveillance, is far removed from the accepted principles of police work. Indeed, it is essentially authoritarian and essentially dangerous.
I ask the minister once more to do something about this. He does not want to give publicity to it. I can understand that. But let Canadians be assured that what has taken place has not been of a nature which will become the pattern for the future. Let them be reassured at the same time that this man will receive the consideration to which every Canadian is entitled.
I should like to know something about him. Apparently he is an immigrant. Whether his name was Spencer when he came to Canada, I do not know. I know nothing of his past except what I have read in the press. Who is he? Where did he come from? How long has he been here? These are things Canadians have the right to know. Set up a judicial inquiry. Let a judicial inquiry look into this matter. There is no reason why the government should not do this. What has been done to date cannot but cause concern to those who believe in the maintenance of freedom within our land.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-STATEMENT AS TO DISMISSAL
speechtext:
The statement which has been made by the Minister of Justice is to my mind astounding in the light of the events which have transpired since May 8. I am sure it will cause many thoughtful persons to be concerned about the way we are administering justice in this country.
I have no brief, nor has any other member of this house, for any person who is guilty of espionage. But under the laws of Canada a man is innocent until proven guilty, and the statement made by the minister this morning is certainly at variance with the statement which was issued by the Department of External Affairs on May 8 last. One paragraph in that statement said that "In one instance a Canadian civil servant was paid thousands of dollars to gather information and documentation in Canada the purpose of which was to assist in the establishment of espionage activities in Canada and in other countries, and to perform economic intelligence tasks including the provision of detailed information on the Trans Mountain Pipe Line system in western Canada."
January 31, 1966

Administration of Justice
That is a clear accusation of espionage and of participation in the setting up of an espionage system in Canada and in other countries. If this is correct the man concerned should certainly be apprehended, tried and, if found guilty, punished. It is significant that this statement was issued by the Department of External Affairs. It is true the department was concerned about the propriety of actions taken by certain Soviet officials and that this was within their proper jurisdiction. But the statement with reference to this particular civil servant makes charges which so far have not been substantiated, and the statement made by the minister today was to the effect that on examination the crown did not have sufficient evidence to stand up in court.
This makes the statement issued by the Department of External Affairs a very strange document indeed. Does it mean that the Department of External Affairs issued its statement without being sure of its ground, or that it released information which had not been carefully documented?
If that is the case, some statement should certainly now be forthcoming from the government to the effect that the accusation against this man was premature and is no longer valid. Instead, what has the government done? First, they fired this man under section 50 of the Civil Service Act so that he has no right of appeal. The minister tells us this morning that this was done after consultation with the Civil Service Commission and on the recommendation of the commission. The body to which this man was to have the right of appeal condemned him before they had even heard him. Was this man permitted to appear before the Civil Service Commission before the commission recommended that he be fired? Or was not this meeting of the Civil Service Commission actually a kangaroo court which made its decision without giving an opportunity to the appellant to appear, leaving a stigma hanging over his head and the heads of his family for the rest of his life?
Is this the way in which justice is to be administered in Canada? Even in wartime we would not permit a man to be stigmatized on the basis of evidence which, as the minister himself claims, would not stand up in court. I say to the government that either they said too much in their statement of May 8, making accusations which they cannot substantiate, or else they are simply making this man a scapegoat for their own ineptitude and inefficiency.

I appeal to the Prime Minister, who has a deep sense of justice in matters of this kind, to reconsider the question. Here is a man who has been accused, first in the statement from the Department of External Affairs and then by the Minister of Justice on a national television program. He has been accused of espionage, but he has been given no chance to prove his innocence. Here is a man who has been dismissed and denied an appeal. In fact he was condemned by the commission before he was given a chance to appeal to the commission. Here is a man who has lost his pension rights; who in all probability will never get another job and who, according to the minister's statement, is to remain under police surveillance as long as he remains in Canada.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
I ask the Prime Minister if he considers this is how justice ought to be administered in this land of ours. Surely the very least the government can do is to agree to the setting up of a judicial committee composed of one or more judges, who would be prepared to hear the evidence which the minister has and decide, first of all, whether this man has been guilty of espionage; second, whether the government was justified in dismissing him and, third, whether in the course of that dismissal he ought to have been deprived of his pension rights. Surely he is entitled, as any Canadian citizen is entitled, to have his day in court. Surely he is entitled to be heard. Surely he has the right under our laws to be deemed innocent until he can be proven guilty.

Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Minister of Justice is surely of widespread interest, for there has been a great deal of comment since May 8, 1965, about these spying activities which took place here in Canada prior to that date, and in which Mr. Spencer was allegedly involved.
But was he the only one involved? We do not know. Was he the mastermind behind it? Again, we do not know.
I am in complete agreement with the suggestion of the leader of the N.D.P. Mr. Spencer should at least be given an opportunity to be heard and to tell his side of the story as clearly as possible. But he is not afforded the slightest opportunity to do so.
It is a very good thing that this spy ring was uncovered and the R.C.M.P. must be commended for discovering this ring which endangered the security of the country.
January 31, 1966

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) mentioned earlier that in such circumstances, R.C.M.P. authorities should refrain from making statements of a political nature when arrests must be made and the law enforced as in the present case.
It has often happened that some members of the R.C.M.P. have made statements of a political nature regarding such arrests.
We approve the steps taken by the government to ensure the security of the state but not when they are prejudicial to anyone, as in the present case for instance when the accused is allowed to state the motives behind his actions so that we may find out whether some one else is involved. In this case, Spencer is precisely being used as an agent. I do not believe that he was the head of this spy ring. There are surely others and more important ones who should be discovered and prosecuted by the Department of Justice.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-STATEMENT AS TO DISMISSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to avoid repetition of what already has been said, surely the Minister of Justice realizes by this time that bungling by the government in the handling of this particular case is not doing very much to establish respect for law and order and confidence in the security of the country. Certainly it is evident that the R.C.M.P. are being made the scapegoat for things over which they have no control. It seems to me that the government owes it to those charged with the responsibility for security in Canada to give them the support that is necessary. No better evidence has been revealed of that need than this particular case which we are talking about.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I come back to this point, that an inquiry is not only essential in this particular case but is also essential in the whole area of security and the enforcement of law and order. This is not just one isolated case. There have been repeated cases to which the public has not had satisfactory answers, cases in which individuals involved have been either let go or charged unfairly.
There should be a full scale inquiry into this particular topic, or at the very minimum the government should issue a white paper on the matter. Over and over again in this house I have urged upon the government the necessity of bringing in some systematic and periodic reports relating to the maintenance of law and order, international crime and espionage activities. Either the mounted police must be given the authority to do so, or
Administration of Justice the government itself, through the Department of Justice, must release this type of information in order that the general public may have the necessary assurance that all is well so far as law and order, international crime and the security of the country are concerned. However, there is no response from the government in this regard.
We as members of the house probably know more about these matters than the general public, but even we are confused because the answers given are not clear. This situation certainly bears out that there is inconsistency and a lack of support from the government to those concerned with law enforcement and security matters.
So, Mr. Speaker, in support of what has already been said, I would urge that an inquiry be made not only into this case but into the whole field, and that some system be devised whereby reports can be given to the country concerning the state of the nation relating to law and order, the inroads being made by international crime, and espionage, and dealing with the whole area of security in the national realm.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister in a position to inform the house and the country regarding the decision of the President of the United States to resume the bombing of North Viet Nam? When did the government of Canada receive this information from the United States administration, and what attitude was taken by the government of Canada in advance of that announcement which has led today to the beginning of another series of bombings in that area?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH VIET NAM-RESUMPTION OF BOMBING BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United States government took the opportunity on January 24 last to inform us that over the period of one month during which the bombing of north Viet Nam had been suspended, and various opportunities taken to explore the possibility of a peaceful solution to the Viet Nam conflict, there had been no response or reciprocal gesture from the other side.
While that message of January 24 did not specifically refer to any decision to resume the bombing, it was made clear that the United States government would regard itself free to review its policies in the light of the failure to elicit a meaningful response from Hanoi. Subsequently-and by subsequently I mean yesterday morning, Sunday-I received a further message indicating the United States government had decided that, in all the circumstances, it had no option but to resume the bombing.
As to the position of the Canadian government, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I have made it clear to this house that the views of the Canadian government on this matter have been fully explained to the United States government through diplomatic channels. The view we took was that we hoped the pause in the bombing might be extended until all reasonable possibilities of bringing this issue from the battlefield to the conference table had been exhausted. We took that position especially in the light of indications that Hanoi might have been giving consideration to the implications of the pause.
However, a message I received this morning from the head of the communist government in North Viet Nam via the Canadian officer in Hanoi, attached to the international
Inquiries of the Ministry commission, indicated that that government was completely intransigent in so far as entering into negotiations was concerned.
The message I received was substantially the same as that which appeared in the press as having been sent to the heads of communist parties throughout the world by the North Vietnamese leaders. It stated, among other things, that there could be no negotiations of any kind until the United States forces withdrew and until they recognized the Viet Cong as the sole government of South Viet Nam.
The position of the United States as stated to us from the beginning has been that they looked upon the pause in the bombing as a step toward peace. As a result of discussions I had on December 29 with the President's special emissary, and as a result of subsequent discussions we have had with United States officials, we believe that the possibility of a further pause is not foreclosed, if and when circumstances suggest that such a pause would be helpful in arriving at a peaceful and fair settlement of this conflict.
I can only say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I expressed to the United States ambassador yesterday that this government regrets that in the eyes of the United States government a resumption of the bombing is necessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice which I consider is probably one of the most important questions I have ever asked. I hope you will bear with me, sir, in this regard.
In view of my responsibility as the member for Vancouver East to protect as far as possible the rights of all my constituents under the laws of Canada, which cannot be interpreted so as to allow an individual to be found guilty of any charge without knowing the charge and without the right to defend himself or herself, will the Minister of Justice

January 31. 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry lay charges against Mr. Spencer, who is alleged to have been an espionage agent, or will the minister appoint a judicial committee to examine all the aspects surrounding this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is anything I can usefully add to that which I have already said in my statement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister give favourable consideration to the suggestion that a judicial body be set up to look into this matter? speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having studied all the facts of this case, I do not feel it is necessary or useful to initiate a judicial inquiry into this matter. The procedures that have been followed by the R.C.M.P. are exactly the same procedures that were followed when my right hon. friend was in the government. As far as the decision not to prosecute is concerned, here again I have studied the matter very carefully in concert with the law officers of the department, and I have arrived at the conclusion that there is not sufficient admissible evidence to suggest a conviction.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext: You sound just like your predecessor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
For the reasons I have outlined no prosecution was initiated.
There is one thing which is perhaps different in this case. Had Mr. Spencer not identified himself no problem would have arisen. He did identify himself, and any inconvenience he has suffered is the result of his own action and not the result or responsibility of the government.

subtopic: GEORGE VICTOR SPENCER-REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
should like to direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister agree that irrespective of how the man was identified, he was fired and identified by that action?

[Mr. Winch.)

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Goyer for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.
Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre)!
Mr. Speaker, in my first speech in this twenty seventh parliament I am pleased to have the opportunity of joining with all those who have spoken during the debate on the Speech from the Throne in offering to you sincere congratulations on your elevation to your present high position. In your capacity as Deputy Speaker in the twenty sixth parliament you showed a wide knowledge of parliamentary procedure and a deep understanding of the working of parliament. I am sure you will continue to act in the same manner in this parliament. I wish also to congratulate the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of Committees. I am sure all members will agree that they are very good choices. I should like also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Goyer) and the seconder (Mr. Stanbury) of the address and wish them both a successful and interesting experience in parliament.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
This is the last day of the debate on the Speech from the Throne. Perhaps it is fitting that the debate should end on such a day of traffic confusion and drifts of snow, because I think those words "confusion" and "drift" well describe the Speech from the Throne outlining the government's legislative program this session. Most of the government's program has drifted into the Speech from the Throne from the last parliament. There appears also to be confusion regarding which legislation will come before us.
There also appears to be a misunderstanding on the part of the public concerning this debate. Many people do not realize that the rules of parliament provide eight days of debate on the Speech from the Throne at the opening of the session. I have tried to inform my constituents at every opportunity that we are not carrying on a time wasting effort but that we are taking a critical look at the program proposed by the government and attempting to offer constructive suggestions for improvement.
Suggestions have been made in various editorial articles and also in the remarks of some hon. members that we should refrain
January 31, 1966

from moving amendments to the address which are considered as being votes of nonconfidence. I cannot agree with these suggestions. If we failed to move amendments in an effort to improve government legislation we would be guilty of avoiding our responsibility as an opposition. I well recall the actions of some of the present occupants of the front bench opposite when they were in opposition during the minority Conservative government of 1962 and 1963. Some of their statements in the house at that time make interesting reading, particularly those of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). I do not have the actual words with me but they were to the effect that it was the duty of the opposition to criticize any government legislation with which it did not agree. If I may recall from memory the words of the Prime Minister-1 was in the house when he said this-he told us it was the duty of the opposition "to try to defeat the government at the earliest opportunity". Nevertheless members opposite now try to say we should not bring in motions of non-confidence.
There is not much one can say on the last day of this debate with regard to the defects of the Speech from the Throne if one is to avoid repetition. But I have a few words to say on a subject of particular interest to my own constituents. This wild day with its drifting snow is a good one on which to bring up the first subject I have in mind. I tried to raise it in the house by means of a question on orders of the day but you ruled me out of order, Mr. Speaker. I trust I can refer to it now. I will begin by reading a statement from the Manitoba Co-Operator. Let me point out that these remarks apply not just to Manitoba but to all parts of the prairies.
The current winter has brought some near record cold spells, plenty of snow, and winds to pile the fluffy white stuff in travel-defying mounds. Individual farmers and municipalities have been hard put to keep their main roads open. Their labors have involved inconvenience, discomfort and expenditures running to the tens of thousands of dollars for snowplowing.
I wish to refer to snowplowing. I have asked the government-there is a question on the subject on the order paper in my name -to consider the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on snowplows. I realize that our motion to have this tax removed entirely on building materials and production machinery was defeated, so I shall not refer to the broader aspect of the question. However, I should like to refer to the 11 per cent sales

The Address-Mr. Pascoe tax imposed on snowplows. This year, farmers found it absolutely necessary to co-operate with their neighbours in forming snowplow clubs. They pooled their financial resources to buy plows. Almost every day this winter it has been necessary to plow in order to keep the side roads open. I have received many letters from my constituents asking for the removal of the sales tax on plows, and in support of this plea I should like to impress upon the government the need which exists for these plows. The comfort, health, safety, and the very lives, almost, of some of the people I represent depend on these roads being kept open.
As for the school children, it is true there are buses to take them to school, but the farmers have to plow their roads before the children can reach the buses. I cannot impress upon the government too strongly the need for removing this tax on snowplows completely.
During the question period another problem was raised having to do with the railways, particularly the cancellation of the Dominion. I know there is an appeal under consideration at the present time and that the cabinet is deliberating this appeal. Last week I drew attention to the fact that the mayors and aldermen of the eight cities on the main line from Calgary to Winnipeg, the others being Portage la Prairie, Regina, Swift Current, Medicine Hat, Brandon and Moose Jaw, met in Moose Jaw last Tuesday. I have here a copy of the minutes of that meeting, received in my mail today. I shall not place all of it on record but there is a great deal of evidence here to indicate how concerned the mayors and reeves are about the discontinuance of the Dominion, a matter to which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) referred when he was out west.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
There are one or two points I should like to emphasize. First, the mayors and aldermen referred to the difficulties of getting to Moose Jaw because of the lack of passenger train service. That was the first point they made. Later they passed a resolution which in part read as follows:
Whereas the Board of Transport Commissioners have not realistically nor objectively assessed the case put by the communities by such abandonment-
That is, to discontinue the Dominion.
Whereas it is absolutely clear that the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing all it can to upgrade the fares and downgrade the service on the Canadian to hasten its abandonment;...
January 31, 1366

The Address-Mr. Pascoe
Therefore be it resolved that this meeting of the cities of Calgary, Medicine Hat, Swift Current, Moose Jaw, Regina, Brandon, Portage la Prairie, and Winnipeg urge the government of Canada to immediately set up a public committee under the direction of the Canadian National Railway passenger department to make an on-the-road survey of passenger train and commuter requirements in all communities serviced by the Canadian Pacific rail lines in Canada.
Then there is this addition to that resolution:
That this meeting make a personal presentation from the cities taking part to the cabinet at Ottawa at as early as possible a date.
I think this fits in with the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition in asking for a full inquiry into the whole matter, and I believe the presentation from these mayors would also fit in with any other presentations which may be made. It was also moved at the meeting that the federal members of parliament who represent the areas affected should be present when the brief is presented to the cabinet. I hope this will be possible and I certainly would wish to be present when the arguments are advanced.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is not in the chamber but I hope he will take note of what I have to say next. I understand there is the possibility of an Easter recess and I thought it would be advisable to make advance reservations on the Canadian, which serves Moose Jaw. I telephoned last week to do so, but already they have a waiting list for suitable reservations on the Canadian during April. This indicates the need for improving the passenger service and I would ask the Minister of Transport to draw the attention of the C.P.R. to the necessity for putting on extra coaches during peak travel periods such as Easter.
I have one or two questions of local interest to mention and one deals with agriculture. I am sure the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) has the Board of Grain Commissioners under his supervision, as did the previous minister. There has been much talk about providing extra quotas to cover tough and damp grain which can be dried and put in shape for marketing. The Canadian government elevator at Moose Jaw, with a Dominion bushel capacity, has the most efficient drying facilities possible, but they are not being used at present. Some way should be found to have portions of this tough grain dried at the Moose Jaw elevator and put into shape so that it may fetch a higher return when it is marketed; and it should be dried at the lowest possible cost.

Last week the Minister of Agriculture took great pride in referring to the latest wheat board statement on delivery quotas. I agree with him that these are improving somewhat but there are some figures for Saskatchewan, from the latest Canadian Wheat Board report which I would like to put on record.
The minister referred to the fact that there were only three points on a one bushel per specified acre quota. But, Mr. Speaker, last year at this date there were none. This year there are 61 points on a two bushel quota. Last year at this date there were none. This year there are 242 points on a three bushel quota. Last year at this time there were only 33. Jumping now to the six bushel quota points, I was pleased to see that there are 196 points on a six bushel quota but I would point out that at this time last year there were 395 points on a six bushel quota. I agree that the minister is probably doing his best to speed up matters but there is still great need for additional boxcars.
Last week the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) made a most interesting speech on automobile safety devices, and I have received a great many letters from my constituents on this matter. They support his statements and have asked me to endorse them in the house, something I am very pleased to do. I shall not read any of the letters but I wish to let you know, Mr. Speaker, that I have received quite a few on this subject.
In this connection I wish to refer to the latest issue of the Highway Safety News which quotes Mr. Bryce, Executive Director of the Canadian Highway Safety Council as saying:
When society accepts the seriousness of the highway traffic situation and demands action, the accident trend will swing downward.
Mr. Bryce makes two or three suggestions, the first of which is:
Train young drivers for 60 years of resourceful driving. No matter how this is accomplished or who does it or who pays for it, this training is a logical and essential step toward reducing road accidents.	^
He also recommends driver improvement courses, and I think everyone will agree this would be one way to reduce traffic accidents. He also recommends motor vehicle inspections. I believe that if a more careful check were made of all cars on the highways it would result in fewer accidents.
Many serious accidents and fatalities occur at railway crossings and it is my opinion that the railway grade crossing fund should be
January 31. 1966

increased and more latitude used with regard to grants made from the fund. In my city of Moose Jaw an application has been made for the elimination of a level crossing and its replacement with an overhead bridge a mile farther down the line. However, the use of the grade crossing fund has been denied in this case because the replacement bridge would not be located at the original crossing. For that reason I maintain there should be more latitude allowed in connection with the use of this fund. In this particular case the elimination of the level crossing would not harm anybody and it would certainly do a lot of good to have it replaced by an overhead bridge.
The Canada Pension Plan fund will be coming up for discussion later in the session and so I shall not say much about it now. However, I would emphasize the great number of letters I am getting and the number of phone calls I received when I was at home, all dealing with the integration or stacking of private pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan. Last year when I questioned this matter the then minister of national health and welfare said it was absolutely a problem for the private pension plans, but I think some direction should be given by the government to assist in the integrating of these plans.
One other point I wish to make in connection with the Canada Pension Plan has to do with the increase in the cost of living resulting from the compulsory payment of premiums which started on January 1. I understand the price of restaurant meals is going up and I should like to refer to one particular case. One small businessman told me he had five fairly well paid employees and one general handyman to whom he did not pay a great deal in wages. When he started figuring out the compulsory payments he had to make on January 1, he realized that his contributions of 1.8 per cent almost equalled the salary he was paying his general handyman. Without compunction he told me he was letting this man go so that the money he had paid him would pretty well equalize the compulsory payments he had to make under the Canada Pension Plan.
Since I have referred to the cost of living I wish to point out that the latest chart issued by the dominion bureau of statistics shows that the cost of living index stood at 140.8 points in December, the highest level on record. The cost of living has been rising continuously and will continue to increase.

The Address-Mr. Pascoe
Hon. members know of the potash developments in my area. The one I am most interested in is only a few miles from Moose Jaw. It is the only one with a solution mining operation whereby water is pumped down and the potash is brought up. I have raised the question on other occasions and I know others have too, but again I emphasize the need for equality of tax treatment for the solution mining method with the treatment that is afforded conventional shaft mining. This is something that has been impressed upon the government on many occasions and I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will bring in some amendment to this effect in the next budget.
The Minister of Finance requested letters from citizens who have views to offer regarding possible budget proposals. I believe he tried to withdraw his request later when he was almost submerged with letters. I should like to draw to his attention one which was sent to me, and I will put it on the record since the minister is not in the house. It reads:
Another suggestion that you might wish to consider would make for more equitable treatment under the Income Tax Act. At present, when a homeowner wishes to sell his house and has to take part of the sale price by way of mortgage or agreement for sale he must report the interest received on his income tax return. However, if he buys a better house or one in a different community, the interest which he pays on the mortgage on the new residence is not allowable as a deduction against taxable income, not even against his interest income arising from the sale of his former residence. It would seem only fair that the interest expense on the new residence should be claimable as a deduction up to the amount received from the sale of the old residence.
Another letter I have just received will be of interest to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith). I have not yet made a request for an answer concerning it. It is from a man who supplies building materials, and in it he says:
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
-in the case of a public or private job, if the contractor does not pay his subcontractor or suppliers they can place a mechanic's lien.
To collect their money:
However, with regard to a government project we understand that a lien is of no value and we were wondering if there is any other recourse.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I intend to follow this up with the appropriate government department but I should also like to put that on record.
I am just clearing away some of these letters I have received. I will not emphasize
January 31, 1966

The Address-Mr. Pascoe the next one too much because it has been dealt with by the government and the answer is no. The letter is from the Federal Superannuates National Association, Regina branch. They ask my support in requesting a revision upwards of the pension for retired civil servants and their widows. I know the government has said no, but we give them fair warning that we are going to carry on the fight in this regard. I think that pretty well clears my desk of letters from constituents, Mr. Speaker.
Now I should like to deal with the major points in the Throne Speech. I have them outlined here. The first is increased grants to universities and a scholarship program for students. We certainly support this program because, as a matter of fact, we started it. The party to which I belong was responsible for the original increase in grants to universities. As I say, we certainly support this program and commend the government for following our example.
The next matter is the extension of crop insurance coverage to make it available to all Canadian farmers. We shall deal further with this question when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture come up for review. Next there is set out in the Throne Speech the federal government's intention to brook no provincial interference in fields of explicit national responsibility. I cannot emphasize this too much, because we are the party that is standing for a strong central government. I am sure we will support this proposal if the government will really live up to their commitments in the Throne Speech.
Next are revisions of the Railway Act. I shall not refer to that question any more because I believe I have impressed upon the house the problems in this connection and what we are going to try to do about them, including the restoration of adequate passenger service.
Next are proposals for the redevelopment of uneconomic farms. This one gives me some cause for concern, because I am a strong advocate of family farms and do not want to see this measure used as a first lever to remove the small family farms. I think some way should be found to increase the earnings of these farmers and leave them on the family farm. I agree that the farms can be redeveloped but I do not want to see the farmers taken off these farms.
Next the government says that it intends to introduce legislation to make "O Canada" the national anthem. I will conclude my remarks

on this topic, Mr. Speaker, because the government seems to have an unhappy ability of dividing this country. They divided it on the flag; they are going to divide it on capital punishment. Now they are going to bring in "O Canada" as the national anthem. I agree with this but believe there should be a national anthem with words that are common to the whole country. 1 do not think we should have two national anthems as we perhaps have two national flags. We should have one national anthem of which we can all be proud and which the people of Canada can sing in all parts of the country. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the house for listening to these few remarks.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, allow me, first of all, to congratulate very warmly my colleagues from the ridings of Dollard and York-Scarborough (Messrs. Goyer and Stanbury) for their speeches as movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I take this opportunity to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your appointment to the speakership of this house. I think that your appointment is clearly a tribute to your bilingualism, a precious advantage which you acquired at the University of Ottawa, one of our country's great bilingual institutions. It is a spontaneous show of respect, and a choice which was never in doubt in the minds of those who are gathered here today.
I also take this opportunity to congratulate your colleague, the Deputy Speaker, and Deputy Chairman of Committees (Mr. Batten).
Mr. Speaker, if I am able today to express sincerely and freely my personal ideas in this house, I must thank the constituents of the beautiful riding of Gatineau, a hunting and fishing paradise, for this honour. The other day in the house, the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette) said that the riding of Villeneuve was the most beautiful. He must have made a mistake, because he decided to come and live in the most beautiful riding, that of Gatineau, to deal with his riding's business.
It is from the bottom of my heart, Mr. Speaker, that I thank my constituents. It is also as their representative, in this assembly, that I shall give my personal views on the medicare program promoted by my government.
Let it be noted, Mr. Speaker, that I am now speaking as an elected member having the
January 31, 1966
right of speech in the parliament of Canada, and not as a member representing the specific interests of a given constituency.
Having been actively engaged for 20 years, in the practice of the medical profession among those who have been, and still are referred to as economically weak, that is the workers and the middle class, and having seen them toil, suffer and die, I think I am qualified to express here a physician's opinion, which is truly Canadian and has little in common with the views of certain paramedical so-called experts, whose only knowledge of sickness and the sick stems from what they read in dusty books found on the shelves of libraries.
If I have often been called to the bedside of a dying man to see him breathe his last after having seen him suffer, it is because people knew that my sympathy extended beyond the physical comfort I could bring. I was aware that illness, for that class of society could mean not only physical decline but hopeless financial ruin.
Our government has already established basic principles which, I think, are quite fair to all the people in Canada. The provinces should adopt them and co-operate with the central government in this respect. Oh, I know quite well that in some circles today people cannot keep from saying no as soon Ottawa has said yes to certain projects.
Such an attitude creates unrest and confusion among the people of certain provinces and it has become a form of snobbery that is in very bad taste from a political standpoint. This should stop, especially when the national welfare is at stake.
It is essential that medicare, as advocated by this government, become a reality in the very near future. People in all walks of life are pressing for it and all are awaiting the implementation of this vast program.
Here, Mr. Speaker, is what we should have in 1967:
First, all Canadians should be looked after and be able to receive equal medical care throughout the country.
Second, the government should assume either complementary or complete responsibility throughout the country with regard to individuals under medical care.
Third, medicare should be instituted not for the benefit of doctors, hospitals, druggists, the government or certain insurance companies, but for the sake of the sick, and that with the full co-operation of those various groups.
The Address-Mr. Isabelle Fourth, such a medicare plan should be portable from one province to another.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

At one o'clock the house took recess.

Do I need to point out, Mr. Speaker, that if health conditions existing 100 years ago had prevailed today, more than half of us here would not have survived.
One out of five would have died in childhood from colic, whooping-cough and typhoid; one out of ten would have been overcome before adolescence by diphtheria, scarlet fever, smallpox or by some of the other quite common diseases attributed to poor nutrition. Among those reaching manhood, one out of twelve would have died before 30 of tetanus, peritonitis or diabetes, or some other illness for which there was no effective treatment. One out of ten would have been stricken before 50 by pneumonia, tuberculosis or other illnesses, but conditions have been greatly improved thanks to medical and pharmaceutical progress.
Those two professions have existed for a very long time, but systematic research really started only in the middle of the nineteenth century. It was, of course, in the following century that therapeutics and preventive medicine made such great strides. Canadians are more and more conscious of the fact that health preservation is an important factor in making life happier and the nation stronger.
According to the 1961 Canada Year Book, Canadians spent, for health purposes, the staggering amount of $1,652 million, that is a little over twice the corresponding figure for 1953.
The point I have been trying to make here, Mr. Speaker, is that if the average life expectancy in Canada now exceeds 70 years, it is because of the prevention of childhood diseases such as those I have just mentioned, and of old age illnesses.
That is why medicare is needed, Mr. Speaker, and especially for those two great classes of citizens, the young and the old. Those should be the first to benefit fully and without cost from health services. Those

January 31, 1966

The Address-Mr. Isabelle should include medical and surgical care, nursing, dental and eye care, including provision of eyeglasses and dentures, drugs and prosthesis. I would even go as far as to suggest to the proper authorities that those comprehensive health services should be extended to any person temporarily unemployed, to the sick and disabled, to people who have a job but who are unable to look after their own needs or those of their family; indeed, all Canadians in need should be covered by a complete health insurance scheme.
How do you expect low income families with children to get proper care in 1966? It is unthinkable and impossible for them to spend money on health care. They must be content with certain free medical services made available to them by the government, for instance, health units and dispensaries.
It is a shame for a flourishing and prosperous country such as ours, to be burdened by so much misery, so many moral and economic frustrations indirectly caused by lack of care resulting in physical impairments.
A recent survey in a few ridings of Ontario and Quebec neighbouring on the federal capital and concerning poverty in the rural classes has opened many eyes. Did you know that at least 70 per cent of those questioned stated they could not afford medical care by a doctor? It is not surprising that these people have physical handicaps and will never be rehabilitated.
Speaking of complete health services for those who need them, there are categories which should be excluded, for instance: single people, families without children or with children over the age required for family allowances. In my opinion, those last groups assume part of the premium. They would be entitled to the same care but they would have made their small contribution to the larger one made by the federal and provincial governments to enable the latter to play their true role as defender of the weak and the poor, as well as a supplementary role among those who are able to live comfortably on this Canadian soil.
I am sure that this extensive plan will fulfil the needs of all classes. In a way, it would be an improvement on the plan now in operation in Saskatchewan, which in my opinion is one of the best in Canada, with regard to health insurance. That plan seems to be working so well that in its October 1965 issue, the Canadian Medical Journal stated that 70 per cent of doctors in that province will vote for

the maintenance of such a plan, whereas a great number of them were opposed to its creation a few years ago.
If my hon. colleague, the leader of the
N.D.P. (Mr. Douglas) says that it costs $24 per person to administer such a plan, I am sure that the government, with its administrative talent, will undoubtedly be able to lower that rate. I ask my hon. colleagues to read in the Canadian Doctor for December 1965, an article by Dr. E. Thompson, honorary president of the University of Saskatchewan, on the Saskatchewan Medical Program.
If, in 1961, Canada had just a little over
21,000	doctors, that is a doctor per 857 inhabitants, the number of our doctors should increase by at least 20,000 before 1991. To train that many doctors before 1991, we will need room for more than 1,000 medical students; larger schools of medicine, grants such as those which our government intends to make to higher education will be needed to contribute, in the near future, to the creation of a Canada stronger than ever, healthier, more anxious to get an education, to live its Canadianism, as we want to proclaim it in 1967.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, allow me to invite all my fellow Canadians throughout the country, wherever they are, to come at least once in their life to Ottawa-it would be better to come when they are young-to visit the Remembrance Hall in the Peace Tower. There they will see words that will make them think, that might have an influence on their whole life. As a matter of fact, life is so mechanized in 1966 that it is almost impossible to stop and think. There on the walls-
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)

I will read this in English although I do not think there is any literal translation of this quotation:
Head how free men throughout this land Kept faith in the hour of trial, and In the day of battle, remembering the Traditions they had been taught, counting Life nothing without liberty.
No provinces are mentioned, Mr. Speaker, only the expression "this land", which means unity through diversity across Canada, this big land of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I begin by adding my words of congratulation to all the members who have preceded me, particularly those who have taken part in debate in this house for the first
January 31, 1966

time. I add my congratulations to the mover of the Throne Speech, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer), and the seconder, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury). The calibre of speeches in this debate has been exceptionally fine. Some very good ideas have been advanced, and I wish those who have brought these ideas forward every success in what is one of their most difficult functions in this house, that of bringing these ideas to fruition. All of us, I believe, come to this house with some wonderful ideas on how things can be improved. The main problem seems to be putting those ideas into effect through legislation. I wish, all members success in seeing their ideas placed on the statute books of Canada.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I wish to congratulate Mr. Speaker on his elevation to the Chair and you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, with whom I have had a most pleasant association during the years we have been here. My good wishes are extended too to the Deputy Chairman of Committees.
Before moving to the main theme of my address this afternoon I wish to mention two matters briefly. One of these is referred to in the Speech from the Throne; the other is not. I refer, first of all, to the statement that legislative proposals will include amendments to the Area Development Incentives Act. The Speech from the Throne does not indicate how this act is to be amended. I have asked the minister whether he can give us any idea of the lines along which this legislation is to be changed.
In reply the minister said merely that this matter was under consideration. I assume, therefore, that no decision has been made. I hope that when the legislation is drafted it will make provision for an extension of this measure so that it may include other types of industry which create employment in various parts of the country. I refer particularly to the tourist industry and to the service industries related to it. The act which has been passed to provide industrial incentives has been effective in the Georgian Bay region of which Parry Sound-Muskoka is a part. At the moment the prospect is hopeful; it looks as though this act may bring a number of industries into the area to assist in its development. One or two firms have begun to make the move and others are inquiring. But many people feel the act could be extended into the area of the tourist industry and in
The Address-Mr. Aiken particular to those parts of the industry whose activities continue throughout the year.
Operators in many parts of Canada are now beginning to develop a year round tourist trade. They are providing facilities for the enjoyment by tourists of our lakes and rivers in summer by catering to those who go swimming or fishing and they are now beginning to provide facilities for skiing and other winter sports. I would ask the minister to consider including this industry when he is considering amendments to this act.
The second matter, one which is not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne at all, concerns Indian affairs. Within the last few years there has been a tremendous acceleration in the demands made by various groups across the country for an improvement in the status of Indians. This comes from sources which have not formerly raised their voices. It is coming strongly from the Indians themselves, much more strongly than for many years. It is coming from both public and private associations.
I am most disappointed that in the Speech from the Throne the government has given no indication that it intends to cope with this problem, one which has been with us for many years and is still with us even though we have made a little progress in dealing with it. It is true an Indians claim commission is to be set up. But it is my view and the view of many others that rather than assist the Indians this will have the effect of wiping out effectively Indian claims which have been in existence for 100 years, by reason of the statutory limitation imposed on claims against the government. It may, of course, deal with some claims but it will do nothing toward a solution of the long term difficulties.
I believe we have to examine, for example, the position of the Indian agent. The existence of this official among Indian bands is evidence of the paternalistic attitude of the government toward the Indians, an attitude which is now becoming rapidly outdated. Most of the Indian agents are doing their best but in some cases they have too much authority and in others too little. I think their jobs should be changed eventually until they are advisers rather than directors. The ultimate end should be the elimination of the necessity for the job of Indian agent so that the bands may become self-governing communities rather than being run from Ottawa through local agents.
January 31. 1966

The Address-Mr. Aiken
Having said this, I think I should turn to my main theme, one which also arises from an omission in the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne fails completely to take notice of the fact that for the fourth time in five elections the government party does not have a majority in the House of Commons. Our constitution is based on the Prime Minister being the leader of the party with the majority in the house. This idea is based in turn on a two party system which assumes that one party is bound to have a majority. In a house with an odd number of members this is presumed to be the case.
With the passing of the years and the emergence of third, fourth and fifth parties the balance contemplated under the constitution has been disturbed. I shall not comment today on whether this is right or wrong. The people of Canada decide whom they want to represent them. They decide on the parties and they decide on the members who are to be sent here. But we have to face the fact that there are third, fourth and fifth parties in this house and that the constitutional balance has been disturbed to the point that in five elections we have had four minority governments.
This has been much to the dissatisfaction of the Canadian people and I think it is time we came to grips with the situation. It is one which did not arise early in our development but it is one to which early consideration must now be given. It should be a normal and accepted practice that parliament should have the right to amend or reject legislation proposed by the government, or any other official act, without the risk of a general election. No government is perfect; I think we can say that with particularly loud voices at the present time. The present government is a clear example of that.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
It is necessary for parliament, if it is to be representative of the people, to have the right to amend or change or reject completely legislation that is unacceptable. Parliament should be able to scold, chastise and reverse the executive branch when it has acted hastily and unwisely. In normal administrative practice, Mr. Speaker, this happens. Many times, as a result of questions put on orders of the day or questions raised on the order paper or motions moved the government decides that a certain action it has taken administratively is wrong and members of the government change their minds without any

fear that they are going to have to resign. Indeed, they will change their minds completely on a course that has been set.
Many times during the last parliament we saw ministers rise and say, "This is the policy. This is it. You will have to accept it." But on further probing, further suggestion and consideration, they came to the conclusion that their first decision was wrong and, to their credit, in many cases their actions were reversed and they accepted that they had been wrong.
If we were to have a government that obstinately refused to change its decisions we would come to the same situation as we have presently in regard to legislation. We would have to vote no confidence in such a government in order to get it out, but I feel there ought to be a middle course and it is that middle course which I am going to suggest today.
We as a house, representing the people of Canada, indulge in somewhat of a defiant and empty gesture when we start off the session by having the Prime Minister introduce Bill No. C-l, which is supposed to indicate that the House of Commons is an independent legislative body. We do not immediately take up the business that His Excellency has suggested but rather we go on with another bit of business. We do that every session to maintain in parliament that right of independent action, to maintain that we are independent from the monarchy and also independent from the executive branch, Her Majesty's advisers.
We go through this procedure. But then we knuckle under to the government when it proposes its legislation with the threat that if we do not do what it says the house can be dissolved. This is particularly true in the case of a minority government. We find that the words "subject to approval by parliament", used by ministers in their statements, are thrown in for technical reasons without those ministers being very much afraid that parliament will reverse them because they know that if parliament reverses them parliament will be dissolved and that will be the end of it. We go through these empty gestures of pretending parliament is supreme even though we know it is not.
This is even more the case with a minority position because the people have spoken differently from what they would have if a majority government had been elected. If a majority is elected we can truly say that the people have spoken, that we have to accept
January 31, 1966

the overwhelming support they have given to the government party and that we have to go along with them. We can fight, delay and sometimes reverse but if the government party insists it can overwhelm us.
But, Mr. Speaker, when the people have sent a minority government to parliament they have spoken just as much as when they send a majority government. They have spoken differently. They have said, we do not have confidence in this or that particular party; we choose to elect our members and let them decide as a body what is the best thing for this country. Therefore we have a decision by the people. It is not that we have to knuckle under to a majority in the house but rather that the house should make its own decisions.
When we put this up against the right of the Prime Minister and the cabinet to recommend dissolution of parliament at any time they see fit, then the whole thing becomes a farce. If parliament does not support the government, the government exercises the right of dissolution and we find ourselves going back to the country again; the people find themselves having to try once again to make up their minds to support a party in parliament, something they have not been able to do on four occasions recently.
The evolution of constitutional power from the monarchy to the people has never got beyond a transfer of this right from the monarch to the cabinet. The so-called supremacy of parliament has been stopped dead in its tracks by the dual practice of allowing the Prime Minister to recommend dissolution of parliament whenever he feels like it and at the same time requiring him to resign whenever his legislation is rejected or even amended against his will.
The series of minority governments which we have gone through in the past nine years have surely shown us something of this basic arrest in our constitutional development. The Americans saw this difficulty when they set up their constitution and they provided for regular elections regardless of the composition of congress in relation to the executive.
The United States constitution provided for some balance between the powers of the executive and the powers of congress. In fact, the Americans saw this problem as far back as the time of the drafting of their own constitution due to the high handed attitude of the monarchy at that time. They did not want to place this power of dissolution in the
The Address-Mr. Aiken hands of the chief executive of their country and so they provided for set elections at regular periods.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we do not need to look to the American constitution as the end-all of democracy. It is not by any means, but I am citing it as an example which has worked out fairly well. In Pakistan there is a fixed term of elections and dissolution by the government is practically non-existent. In India we find that the practice of regular four-year elections is the norm, and starting in 1967 I understand their term of parliament will be fixed so that no person can change the timing of an election except under unusual circumstances. In my view we should follow this practice in Canada so far as our constitution permits.
We no longer have an absolute monarchy in Canada but the powers of the monarch to dissolve parliament exist just as strongly now as they did 200 years ago because they are still resting in the hands of the executive branch and of the Prime Minister. I do not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that minority governments are a good thing but under proper constitutional practices they can be made to express the will of the people; they can be the perfect embodiment of the principle of the supremacy of parliament.
Without rejecting the fundamentals of our constitution we can take a long step forward toward freeing ourselves from the last remnants of an absolute monarchy, now held by the cabinet and the Prime Minister, by taking out of the hands of any individual the right to dissolve the people's parliament at will and transferring it to parliament itself. In so doing we would not be casting our constitution into any rigid formula. I am not proposing a system of fixed term elections such as those in the United States, India and Pakistan that I have mentioned but I am proposing that we move to correct this fundamental defect in our constitution. I believe it should take the form of an amendment to the British North America Act. Such an amendment can be made by this parliament without reference to any other authority because it affects merely the sittings of parliament itself.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
In summary, I should like to see an amendment to our constitution with the following objectives in mind: First, as an immediate means for the prevention of any further election in the near future and, second, to provide us with the authority to amend or reject government legislation from
January 31. 1966

The Address-Mr. Aiken time to time without the threat of an election. Third, I should like to see parliament vested with the ability to bring about an election when and if the government has lost the confidence of this house, most especially when there is a minority government in power. Fourth, I should like to see the elimination of the right of the prime minister to recommend dissolution at his own will, thus settling that problem of which all of us are aware, which has been left over since the year 1926.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will pay particular attention to my last two points. I should like to have a more definite term for the existence of a parliament and finally, all these things should be encompassed within the framework of our constitution.
This may sound like a tall order but I think we can accomplish these objectives by amending section 50 of the British North America Act and adding a subsection 50(a) perhaps which might state that, notwithstanding any custom or usage which now exists, no government shall be deemed to have been defeated in the House of Commons by rejection or amendment of any government legislation or otherwise save by a general vote of non-confidence at times to be established in the rules, and that no prime minister shall recommend to His Excellency the dissolution of parliament within a period of four years after polling day in a general election save as the result of such general vote of non-confidence.
It is my intention to bring in a bill along these lines when my research has been completed and after there has been some discussion of these particular problems. I make these suggestions now because many people in this country have become concerned with these problems and are thinking seriously of how we should correct our constitution to deal with the situation as it exists now in this mid-twentieth century. Perhaps there could be some private and public discussion of these suggestions followed by some direction for future action.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the government itself should make proposals to start the ball rolling in respect of our constitution without concerning itself only with technicalities and problems in respect of English-French relations and provincial-federal relations. We must begin to think more definitely about these problems and


about how they can be solved rather than about philosophies which may lead us nowhere.

Mr. Speaker, if I may do a disservice to a familiar quotation, this might be one of the days of this session during which an ill wind did nobody any good because if the weather had been finer I would not have been speaking today.
I should like to congratulate you, sir, on your exaltation to the Chair you now occupy. I have had the opportunity of observing your performance in the past parliament and I congratulate you and I congratulate ourselves. In times past I have expressed my view in respect of the eminent qualifications of the Speaker of this parliament. I am delighted that he is living up to the fine predictions so many of us made for him. It is with no perfunctory purpose in mind that I congratulate the hon. members who so eloquently and thoughtfully moved and seconded the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Once again I find that I have made quite a move in this chamber. During the former parliament I was seated as close as one might get to Mr. Speaker on the far right of the second row. I now find myself on the extreme left of the same row. This would indicate that no man can move as much as I have and progress as little as I have as a result of this move. It also, I may say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), would indicate that this "right-left" terminology is utterly meaningless in a Canadian parliament. I have not moved one inch to the left, politically speaking.
The Speech from the Throne, whatever else it may not be, is certainly one of the most lengthy documents that has ever occupied that prime place in any legislative body. Not long ago, for the sake of curiosity I was looking at past Speeches from the Throne. I found that many of them were encompassed in the space of a single column of Hansard and many, indeed most, only required a portion of two columns. Whether we have become more verbose or whether governments are more prolific in their words or whether our problems are becoming multitudinous, I do not know, but we now require five columns of fine print to set forth that prime document.
The Throne Speech is an old document in the sense that much of what is stated in it has been stated many times before. I hope
January 31. 1966	COMMONS DEBATES
that if nothing else is done during this particular session we can sit at least long enough with sufficient government direction and timing so that many of these ancient promises will be enacted, allowing something new to be stated in upcoming Throne Speeches, whoever should write them.
Whatever we have done in recent sessions, and we have begun well this session, we have done something to improve our procedures and their relationship to that large batch of legislative fare now before us. The size of that fare must certainly indicate that we should be aware of the necessity to improve our procedures.
During the last session I made a suggestion which was not acted upon. This does not surprise me because one becomes used to having his good ideas ignored. At that time I thought and said that it was shocking to know that we were wasting so much time not on what we were discussing, because I would never say on listening to any hon. member's views that his utterances were a waste of time, but because I am always impressed by the great time waster in this chamber, the amount of time which we allow to lapse after we decide to vote and the taking of the vote.
I have had a little compilation made in respect of votes taken during the few years I have been a member of this chamber, beginning with the twenty third parliament which now seems to be so long ago. I have had a little table made as to the number of votes that have been taken and the number of hours that have been spent in polling the vote and in waiting for the vote to be polled.
