I have discovered that in the time which elapsed before the beginning of the twenty third parliament and the beginning of the final and rather suddenly decapitated session of the other, 125 hours were devoted by hon. members to sitting in the lobby or somewhere else waiting for a vote to be taken. This was the equivalent of 22 sitting days as our days were then structured. This is an appalling waste of time and I suggest again that we consider our system of voting. I am prompted to do so by the fine renovations which have been made in the chamber. Although the Fowler commission was concerned with this matter in regard to radio, one can hardly say that it is a matter of the same concern to a parliamentary body but we are interested in

Mr. Speaker, it is never my nature nor my desire to be purely negative in discussing public matters but it is difficult at times to be very positive when one is concerned, as one must be, about the performance of the government now in power. I should like to begin my few remarks by commending what was in the Speech from the Throne in reference to education and in particular the way in which that was developed by the specific announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) some time later. It is not so long ago at all, Mr. Speaker, that a very small per capita grant was given to the universities. It was a dollar when I came to this parliament. The government which I supported doubled it. Now it has been raised to $5. This is an excellent, worthy move and the beginning, I hope, of a massive consideration of the need for aiding education from whatever level of government such aid can be extracted-and I use the word "extracted" deliberately and advisedly.
The $7 million that was being made available in 1951 and 1952 will now rise to $100 million and beyond. It is just a beginning, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to re-fight the election here, although the last was one of the most pleasant I have been through, not just because of the result but the whole campaign, but our party believed, and said so in the campaign, that the grant should be raised to $5. We also were impressed, as the educational leaders have been impressed, with the need for special assistance to the maritime universities, these fine institutions of learning which have a far greater out-of-area student population than most other institutions in the country.
I am glad that some consideration of this need is being recognized. I believe that our suggested formula was more clearcut and I think the results would have been more helpful, but at this time I do not intend to cavil about the formula.
Grants of this kind, let us recognize it, are but a commencement. I read in a Canadian Press dispatch just the other day a casual review of the problems facing universities, and it was revealed in this item that at the present moment our Canadian universities have actually on their drawing boards or under construction $500 million worth of new buildings. Even when those are completed we

It would be a cliche to say, though many economic documents in non-rosy language are bringing this more and more to our attention, that the training and educating of our young people is indeed our number one investment, even in crude economic terms if in none other. The constitution notwithstanding, the federal government has become importantly involved in the field of education, and this must be recognized.
I was delighted with this splendid document, the Second Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada, one of the most helpful documents I think we have had in a long time. I was delighted and impressed by the way in which this document pointed up and underscored the importance of educational training in the development of our industrial, economic and leadership capacity. This document also impressed me by the perceptive way in which it discussed something which is very, very old and which is very, very close to the hearts of people who live in my part of Canada. I refer to the painful economic disparity in the Atlantic province area which has long endured and continues to endure.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that none of us had to be told that the personal income of the people of the maritimes lags far below that of the rest of Canada. At page 101 of this report

Must we always have unemployment twice as bad, must all the indices of economic prosperity be lower? Was that what was in mind when less than 100 years ago there was a union of the then separate communities to form a new and greater whole? If anyone wants to know the main reason the Atlantic regions did not contribute to the Prime Minister's desire for a majority government, he has only to look at the records of the parties when in office. No government has yet seized the initiative in the manner in which the government of 1957 did when it was recognized that special needs required special measures. It was for that reason the people who supported that government were not forgotten by the voters of the Atlantic regions.
These, Mr. Speaker, are difficult times. I read that the Prime Minister said Canada was a hard country to govern. Sir John A. Macdonald said that a long time ago. It was true then and it is true now. These are difficult times. Some of the eld problems recur in forms which appear to be new. Once again, we are concerned in a special way about the separation of the parts from the whole. The centrifugal forces which would draw away the parts from the centre have always been present. Indeed, at the time of confederation there were many well intentioned people who thought that the coalescence of the parts was

not a good thing. Nova Scotia was wholeheartedly against confederation. Prince Edward Island was against it as long as it could be. New Brunswick was not enthusiastic. The members from Canada east in the old Canadian legislature were, I believe, split about 50-50. We have, however, survived all the trials.
Our first Prime Minister spent most of his career fighting off the incursions of the provinces and the provincial leaders. I think we are perhaps in more difficult times now than ever before. I say it very simply, and I say it sincerely, that my concern stems from the fact I do not believe that the people who are charged with responsibility for the central government are aware of the danger or, if they are, they are most inept in preserving unimpaired the role of the central government. I have often said in this house, Mr. Speaker, that it used to be considered fair political gain for the provinces to gang up on the dominion government, and that quite often opposition groups in parliament at Ottawa pursued their political advantage as they saw it by siding with the provinces and assaulting those in charge of the dominion government. However, this is the first government in history which itself seems to be on the side of the provinces. At dominion-provincial confrontations, one after another, it would seem that the provinces emerge as the victors.
We have now dominion-provincial conferences of one kind or another practically every day. We have never had so many. Sometimes we find out what went on if the provincial participants, when they get back to their provinces, choose to tell us. The only thing that is disturbing about this is that they do not speak with very much unanimity as to what occurred. I feel that perhaps it would be better, instead of having so many dominion-provincial conferences, if this government took the time to prepare itself for some of them. It is obvious from the little information we do get that our dominion people do not go there very well prepared. I would say to them that the time has come to abandon this secrecy broken only by a belated press release or a sensational utterance from a provincial minister.

I think the whole procedure should be rationalized. Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of the Speech from the Throne it is customary for each speaker to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. In this case I am convinced-and I know the house will agree with me-that if this rule had not existed, each and every one of the members who made a contribution to the debate would nevertheless have wanted to extend their enthusiastic congratulations to the mover, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer), and to the seconder, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury). Indeed, both of them discharged their duty with objectivity and talent and in a conscientious manner. Each made a speech in which seriousness did not exclude zest, but in which zest did not exclude seriousness.
To the House Speaker and to you, I also wish to extend my congratulations-here again, not to respect tradition, but because they come straight from the heart-on your respective elections. Like all the other members, I shah pray God to help you with your decisions and I promise you my full support in the discharge of your duties.
Last Thursday, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) gave us one of the great tragi-comical performances the house has come to expect from him. The press reported that he was at his best and, indeed, he had called upon all his assets as an accomplished actor.
Usually, Mr. Speaker, one does not answer a monologue at the theatre, one merely applauds in recognition of the actor's talent and the beauty of his performance. However, in his monologue of last Thursday, the Leader of the Opposition went further; he claimed to be asserting certain truths which, in fact, were totally distorted. That is why I would be shirking my responsibilities if I did not, before the end of the debate, rise in an attempt to state the case clearly.
January 31, 1966	COMMONS
Feigning anger and indignation, as he often does, the Leader of the Opposition, used as a pretext-and I insist on that word-the speech I gave on the evening of January 22, in Montreal, to a group of Liberal students, to assert, all the while distorting the meaning, that I was in collusion with certain Quebec government authorities, and more specifically with the Quebec premier, to suggest discarding the formula for the amendment of the constitution and to arrange so as to cast the odium of that decision on the Conservative party. To support the theory he was building up that night, he made a great to-do over a letter dated two days earlier, that is January 20, 1966, and addressed to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) by the Quebec premier, a letter in which the latter stated that his government, and I quote:
-has decided to postpone indefinitely the consideration of the proposal for constitutional amendment.
In other words, the Leader of the Opposition asserted more or less that Mr. Lesage had written to the Prime Minister of Canada on January 20 advising him of the decision of his government to postpone indefinitely consideration of the proposal for constitutional amendment. And aware of this fact, the President of the Privy Council went to Montreal to suggest precisely the same thing and, by doing so, to throw all the blame for it on the Conservatives and their colonial attitude.
Mr. Speaker, I must say very clearly and very strongly that this conclusion, or rather this accusation made by the Leader of the Opposition shows-if you want to use a more charitable expression-an erroneous interpretation of the facts, and the premise on which it is based could not be farther removed from the truth.
Anyone who takes the trouble to read objectively-and without any desire to find fault with it-my speech of January 22, should understand, if he can read, if he puts each sentence in its true context, that this speech has nothing to do with a government's decision, whatever it is, to put off indefinitely examination of the Fulton-Favreau formula.
As a matter of fact-and it is important not only to point it out but also to remember it-the speech did not deal in any way with the formula, its contents, the desirability of adopting or not adopting it, or of postponing it; it dealt essentially with the danger there would be in acting too quickly not in adopting the amending formula, but in amending

The Address-Mr. Favreau or reshaping our constitution. In other words, my speech even presupposed the repatriation of the constitution, because how is it possible to recommend precautions in amending a constitution if one does not already have at its disposal the tool to make those amendments?

And this is where an essential distinction arises, of which the Leader of the Opposition is well aware he who claims to be jurist, he who caused a similar formula to be submitted to a federal-provincial conference by his Minister of Justice when he was head of the government, he who is fully aware of the distinction, failed nevertheless to emphasize it when he should have. There is a world of difference between the amending formula of a constitution and the amendment to the constitution.
The amending formula is a device, a tool, an instrument used to operate a revision of the constitution. The amendment itself is the result obtained from the application of the formula I mentioned, that is to say the series of constitutional changes on which agreement can be reached by Canada and the provinces during consideration of the great charter by which we are governed.
The crux of the whole matter I was discussing is to be found on pages 4 and 5 of the document I had distributed at the request of some members of the house. I quote:
I now raise the most difficult question a politician ever had to answer: does the social, economic and cultural progress of Quebec require a revision in depth of the British North America Act? Is it essential, in order to ensure Quebec's development in accordance with its traditions and its own aspirations, to disrupt the whole constitutional system?
There is no reference to the formula here.
The most logical answer I can give is that we still do not know to what extent it is possible to make use of the letter and the spirit of the British North America Act. so as to promote the development of Quebec and the other provinces.

Hundreds of students are now anxious to know whether they will be able to find jobs during the summer holidays so that they can help their parents meet the cost of their continuing studies. In our area, reforestation work could be launched.
If there is one thing on which everyone agrees in my area, it is that in many instances our forests were devastated when rational logging operations should have been the rule; they have not been reseeded as they should have been when they were razed by fire.
As a result of this want of foresight, nay, of this carelessness, today our forests worthy of large scale operations are less and less accessible. More often than not preserves are located hundreds of miles from processing centres which increases operating costs.
On the other hand, important forest preserves located near logging areas have been plundered. The supplementary income the farmers got from them for a long time is not coming in any more: the natural resource has disappeared.
Finally, forests which should never have been cleared were sacrificed to colonization with well-known results.
All this shows that a natural and renewable resource, one of the most important at our disposal, did not sufficiently engage our attention with regard to its renewal.
It is high time to restore our forests in the areas which are suited for such a purpose and which are, so to speak, near at hand.
The restoration of the forests means to give the farmers a supplementary income would certainly meet the wishes of the farming community which finds itself now in a very difficult economic situation.
However, we should this time avoid the mistake of allowing such woodlots to become depleted, and we should ensure their rational management.
January 31, 1966	COMMONS
No doubt the costs of such an operation should be considered in the main as capital expenses aimed at rebuilding our national heritage, but it is to be expected the jobs created thereby, while reducing unemployment, would help lower the costs of social assistance in the area.
The implementation of such a plan would require all types of workers but would especially offer an outlet for workers who are unable to qualify for industrial jobs that are becoming more and more technical. At the same time, a most acute social problem would be minimized.
As regards farming problems, and they are many, I hope the government will try to provide logical and practical solutions.
We seem to have forgotten in the past that agriculture was but a part of a much more complex whole. Efforts were made to cure the affected part without bothering to re-establish circulation throughout the system. We failed to go to the heart of the problem by not paying enough attention to the human element. We sacrificed the individual, either the farmer or the worker, in the name of economics, efficiency and technique. There is a great deal of unrest in farming circles because the promotion of efficiency has been done at the expense of the farmer and to the benefit of other classes of society. While the farmer is being asked to double and triple his production, is the doctor looking after more patients than 20 years ago, the lawyer handling more cases than before? Is the newspaperman writing more articles than he did during the depression? Certain trades or professions are not producing more today than in the past, and yet their income has increased substantially. Why apply two different standards?
We are here to try and find, through appropriate legislation, fair solutions to the problems of today. With this in mind, the co-operation of members of this house should be assured.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of a party which long has been interested in the conservation and proper development of our natural resources by Canadians and for Canadians I was amazed to find no reference to the urgent need for a national water policy in the Speech from the Throne, particularly in view of the public interest in this important question both before and during the election.
DEBATES	461
The Address-Mr. Herridge
Prior to proceeding with my remarks on this issue I wish to make a few comments on the speech made on Thursday, January 27, by the hon. Member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) in which he came out in wholehearted support of the New Democratic party's national water policy. Without doubt, during his absence from this house he has had an opportunity for reflecting upon this issue. No doubt he is also aware of the growing public support for the policy announced by this party before and during the election. I must say I congratulate the hon. member for Kamloops on seeing the light with regard to this important question at last. I admit he has informed me that this was his party's policy in 1946. This is why some of the members of his party in Kootenay West have designated his stand on the Columbia treaty as "Fulton's Folly".
The hon. member has followed a tortuous path on this issue. In the first instance he supported the Columbia River Treaty as designed to meet the wishes of Premier Bennett. Later, in his Prince George speech with reference to Premier Bennett's proposed long term sale of downstream benefits, he said this was the greatest sellout since the Indians sold Manhattan island for a bottle of whisky and that accepting such a proposal would make us the laughing stock of the world. But when the same hon. member appeared before the External Affairs committee while it was discussing the Columbia River Treaty he said that he had felt all along that the treaty was an advantageous one for Canada.
I admit the hon. member for Kamloops has been a tortured soul since 1961. It has been a contest between policy, conscience and political expediency. And expediency won. However, once again I congratulate him on his complete conversion to the national water policy of the New Democratic party.
In view of the public interest taken in this issue during the election many people are wondering why this important question was overlooked in the Speech from the Throne. Soon after the Columbia River Treaty was signed the United States authorities revealed the truth about water shortages in the United States as a result of the pollution of rivers and lakes in that country, a situation which has now reached crisis proportions. Egged on by the population upsurge which is now approaching the 200 million mark, there is now a growing interest in that country in Canada's attractive water supplies.
I am one who has always contended that we cannot maintain or improve our standard
January 31, 1966

The Address-Mr. Herridge of living unless we develop and conserve our natural resources. I am sure there is an umbilical connection between the welfare of people and the development of natural resources within any nation.
Seeking to capitalize on the growing water crisis in the United States, an American engineering firm, Ralph M. Parsons Company of Los Angeles, has come up with an imagination-boggling one hundred billion dollar scheme to build interconnecting international waterways so that water would flow from the heartland of western Canadian headwaters in northern British Columbia and the Yukon and also from Alaska southward to the arid parts of the United States and Mexico. This scheme is known as North American Water Power Alliance. To indicate the interest which this proposal has created in the United States and Canada I should like to quote one or two statements which have been published in various periodicals. The first is by J. M. Minifie, from the Commentator of November, 1965, page 22:
Interest in Canadian water is much more acute than interest in Canadian politics. It has only recently come to American attention that God, through some unbelievable lapse into absentmindedness, endowed not God's country but Canada with four fifths of the continent's fresh water. Vast schemes are now being studied to repair God's mishandling of the continental water supply, and re-route streams running into the Arctic, Hudson's bay and Pacific north of the forty ninth parallel, to a more southerly debouchement, to insure that every American kid gets a glass of fresh water.
General McNaughton gave this vision the royal Canadian raspberry by recommending that the United States clean up its own abundant but dirty water before demanding clean Canadian water.
Again, to indicate the interest there is in this question I wish to quote Mr. Kenneth McNaught from Saturday Night of December, 1965, at page 15:
It was unquestionably due to the deliberate blurring of the problems of Canadian-American relations that General McNaughton was able, in one speech, to expose the bankrupt policy underlying the old parties' fear of issues involving nationalism. Pointing directly to the danger of believing the myth of unlimited Canadian natural resources, and to the growing attention being paid to our fresh water reserves by American corporations which have succeeded in polluting billions of gallons of their own water, he issued one of the gravest warnings Canadians have heard in recent years. Noting the proposal to form "a monstrous corporation calling itself NAWAPA" to drain water from the Rocky Mountain trench and distribute it across the continent at a cost of a hundred billion dollars, McNaughton underlined the implications of this kind of continental development. Basically they are that we would hand over water, as we have handed over oil and other resources, to the

planning of giant American companies whose interest in the balanced growth of a Canadian economy is non-existent.
The political implications of selling out our last and greatest resource are no less important than the economic. If, as McNaughton said, our north is to be developed by Canadians, the result will be to add not only economic strength, but a depth arising from the diversity of cultures and political traditions that will enrich as well as strengthen the whole of North America. This to my mind is a true concept of continental development.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Farther on, he continues:
The scandalous lack of clear policy statements on water policy was simply an extreme example of the Issue evading of the whole election. For this, Canadians have paid by electing a parliament whose claim to be truly representative must be at best implausible. Perhaps, just as the election of 1911 followed that of 1908, we will eventually face issues during a campaign.
Neither of the two old parties has a water policy. One has only to look at the maudlin statements made by speakers for both those parties.
The biggest mistake of the major parties was to avoid deliberately live, real issues during the election. However, in spite of their efforts one vital issue, the need for a national water policy, was forcefully injected into the campaign not by a politician but by a private citizen known as General Andrew McNaughton, who is respected as one of the most colourful and dedicated patriots in Canadian history and who has devoted his whole life to building lasting material into the foundations of the Canadian nation.
He has never hesitated to direct his fire at wavering politicians when a national issue was at stake and his current campaign to preserve Canadian water for future generations of Canadians may well rank as the most important of his many contributions to our country. Without a doubt, Mr. Speaker, his dramatic introduction of this issue into the recent election put some significance into what we considered an unnecessary election campaign.
Because of his great concern with this issue General McNaughton made an outstanding address on the need for a national water policy to the annual meeting of the Engineering Institute of Canada last May. Time does not permit me to deal with the contents of this speech but I urge every member of the house who is interested in the problem to obtain a copy from the Journal of the Engineering Institute of Canada. When General McNaughton had concluded his remarks on that occasion he received a standing ovation
January 31, 1966

from all the delegates present at the annual meeting, and since then he has received tremendous support from engineers and organizations interested in the problem.
Later he gave a similar address on October 4 to the Canadian Club at Montreal which brought this subject to the attention of the Canadian people and made it an issue during the election. What was the reaction of the press to this speech? I shall refer to some press comments briefly. I quote from the Victoria Times of October 18:
Prime Minister Pearson must make an early clarification of his comment that he plans to discuss export of Canadian water with United States interests. He should make it very clear that, while he may not be adverse to talking about it, he can have no intention of letting any of this vital resource be diverted out of Canada with or without recompense.
Again, from the Victoria Colonist of October 19:
It is a rather strange spectacle when the leaders of the two largest political parties in Canada are not only at odds with each other on the question of water export, but at variance also with colleagues of their own. Thus we are left in doubt as to the policy of either party, which serves only to emphasize the recent warning of General Mc-Naughton that Canada is proceeding in a political vacuum. His point was that programs shaped by special interest groups can get out of control for lack of a firm national purpose and that Canada should look to its future development before starting international studies. The warning is surely worth heeding.
The Calgary Herald of October 4 shows the nation-wide interest in this question:
It certainly appears that the lack of a formally enunciated Canadian policy on water is encouraging U.S. interests to press for adoption of a vast scheme to divert Canadian water. Until these interests are persuaded by an unequivocal declaration that we have no intention of falling for the continental water-supply proposal, the pressure will increase. Canadians should not be asked to put severe limitations on the potential development of this country because of U.S. inertia in dealing with a problem of cleaning its own house.
The Calgary Albertan of October 7:
If, as General McNaughton says, the U.S. is not short of water but merely short of unpolluted water, there is no need for us to inject neighbourly sentiment into the formulation of our policy.
Then again, the London Free Press of October 14:
The timing of McNaughton's blunt speech was ideal in that it has resulted in a debate on the hustings about a subject too little discussed and too little recognized as one of the most fundamental of all-for the ultimate extent of national development hinges upon the availability of uncontaminated water.

The Address-Mr. Herridge
The Kingston Whig-Standard of October 13 said:
More and more, with some additional help from nature in the form of droughts, people on this continent are coming to realize that water is their most precious resource. In a speech the other day, General McNaughton, one of the few prominent Canadians who has always recognized the great danger of giving away our resources without really knowing their true value or the needs of future generations, advised the Americans to "clean up your own pollution and you'll have plenty of good water." It must be encouraging to General McNaughton to know that finally his views are beginning to receive the attention they deserve in this country-and in the United States.
It was an American who put this whole problem in its right perspective the other day. Abel Wolman was quoted in the St. Louis Post-Disvatch as follows: "The prophets of water shortages fail to grasp the fact that ample water is available (in the U.S.), that it can be collected and transmitted quite inexpensively, and that intelligent conservation and management are the prerequisites to safety. Hysterical recourse to fanciful substitutes and wasteful alternatives is certainly unwarranted for the foreseeable future."
What was the reaction of the political parties to this very important question? Well, this was the first reaction from the Prime Minister on October 15:
We have lots of water___We will be discussing
this with the U.S., who are very anxious to work out arrangements by which some of our water resources are moved down south. This can be one of the most important developments in our history.
The same right hon. gentleman was quoted in the Toronto Star on October 26-no doubt he had time to think the matter over and had heard from some of his own candidates in the election-as follows:
-in the long range future a surplus of water might permit export, but certainly that will not be in the immediate future. Export can be considered only after we have worked out our own national water policy.
He tempered his policy a bit there, I suppose as the result of protests from within his own party.
What did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) have to say? On October 16 he said:
The government appears willing to pull the plug on one of our most vital resources. The Conservative party will not agree to a continental diversion plan. This would mean the chipping away of Canadian sovereignty.
Then, according to the Globe and Mail of October 25 he said:
The Conservative party's national water policy calls for the diverting of northern rivers to supply southern Canada. Mr. Diefenbaker made this clear Saturday night. He did not explain how, if northern waters are diverted to the great lakes, the U.S. could be prevented from tapping the lakes.
January 31. 1966

The Address-Mr. Herridge
Now we come to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing). On October 18 he said:
Diversion of Canadian water to the U.S. is not negotiable. There is no such thing as a continental resource. We own it.
On October 28 he said:
If (the U.S. should become starved for water) we certainly would not sit idly by when we have 40 per cent of the world's fresh water. It is not our intention to dispose of water without first investigating all alternative uses.
Evidently the minister had a chat with the Prime Minister and they reconciled both their previous statements.
What about the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton)? On October 8, in a press interview at Nelson, he made this statement:
Canada should agree to a U.S. plan to build a series of canals to carry fresh water from northern Canada to parched areas of the U.S. In return, Canada should be guaranteed a 15 per cent annual growth rate for the steel industry, which would eventually give Canada half the North American output.
Could you ever imagine anyone attaching a national water policy to the customs tariff based on the rate of production of steel?
Then, according to the Globe and Mail of October 25:
Instead of selling water, Mr. Hamilton proposed that the industries in the U.S. that use extensive supplies of water and energy should plan their future expansion in Canada where the water already exists.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
No doubt the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) had a chat with his leader and they reconciled their positions. The whole thing is that it is clear that neither the government nor the opposition at this time, with the exception of individual members such as the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) who has come out in strong support of our policy, have a national water policy.
What about this party? Our party has a national water policy which was adopted at our national convention held in Toronto last year. I might say that we had a national water policy when the Columbia River Treaty was before this house and that is why this party opposed it. In addition to that, provincial conferences held in British Columbia and Saskatchewan have adopted resolutions which support the principles enunciated by General McNaughton in his speech to the Engineering Institute of Canada and the Montreal Canadian Club. That has been our stand from the start and particulary since this became a vital issue before this house.

I should like to quote the resolution adopted by the last Saskatchewan convention of our party, because this is the one I have at hand. It encompasses the principles that we have been advocating for years. The resolution states:
Resolved that we support the principles of General McNaughton for water control in Canada, which include insistence on Canadian autonomy in development and control of water resources, with Canadian needs receiving priority.
Therefore our leader and our candidates during the election were able to explain clearly and forcefully our approach to this question. There was no hesitation on our part in this regard. We are the only party in this house that has a national water policy and, furthermore, we were able to explain it. We did not arrive at this policy over night. It was arrived at by a democratic procedure. We had committees at provincial and national conventions which discussed this whole problem years ago. As a result of the recommendations of these committees our national water policy was devised and adopted.
There is wide support in the press across the country for General McNaughton's point of view. I pay tribute to the periodicals that have expressed their interest in this important question and supported in principle the suggestion that we should have a national water policy in Canada and that Canadian interests should receive first attention. I mention the Family Herald, the Financial Post, the Financial Times, the Western Producer, the Canadian Wildlife Federation and many other dailies and other periodicals. I have not time to mention them all at this time but I have collected and read most of them and I am glad that many weeklies, dailies and other periodicals are following this question closely.
Canadians have sound reasons to be fearful of the government's lack of policy on this issue; first, because of the recommendations in the report by Mr. A. D. P. Heeney and Mr. Livingston T. Merchant on Canada and the United States, principles in partnership, and I should like to quote section 81:
It is in the abiding interest of both countries that, wherever possible, divergent views between the two governments should be expressed and if possible resolved in private, through diplomatic channels.
What does it mean? It means behind the scenes; it means the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) will again have the opportunity to present to this house and to a committee another treaty and say: Here it
January 31, 1966

The Address-Mr. Herridge
In Vancouver during the election campaign the Prime Minister made a broadcast in which he opposed this arrangement. He also sent a letter to the chairman of the Arrow Lakes Water Resources Committee which stated, and this is fixed in my mind almost like chapters in the Bible:
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
No Liberal government will ever sign a treaty-on the Columbia until it has consulted with the people of the Arrow lakes who are directly concerned.
Did you ever hear of any consultation, Mr. Speaker? We never did. Once again, I often wonder what the late C. D. Howe would say about the signing of this treaty. We knew his attitude; he supported the former coalition government's stand in British Columbia that we should not permit the building of the Libby dam. He also supported General McNaughton on this issue and at General McNaughton's suggestion he introduced the International Rivers bill. There has been a great departure from his policy in recent years.
Competent Saskatchewan authorities have claimed that this water would be worth $20 per acre foot for use in the development of industry for that province. The large-scale consumptive use of water is essential at this time to the development of agriculture and industry in Canada, particularly in the prairie provinces.
We are also concerned to note that water resources will now come under the jurisdiction of the minister of the new department of energy, mines and resources. In this connection I wish to quote from The Reporter of January 27, 1966, an article written by Dillon O'Leary. This is very interesting, and I quote briefly:
And yet there are faint signs in Ottawa of a thaw in water-export policy. During the campaign, Pearson talked of exporting water as a commodity like wheat or oil, though he hedged by adding that this would be considered only after Canada's own requirements were secured. His post-election cabinet and administrative reorganization hinted that there might be a subtle change in the official line. The administration of water was taken out of Laing's Department of Northern Affairs and entrusted to a new department of resources and energy headed by a reputedly bright political novice, Jean-Luc Pepin. In appointing Pepin, Pearson emphasized the need for a national water policy.	.
Pepin displays none of Laing's unyielding approach. In a recent interview he talked of his position on the water-export controversy: "We are going to develop our resources to use them in the national interest, and if in using them in our own


interest we find they can also be used in the American interest as well, we shall do that." Moreover, he does not believe that Canada should reject all American approaches until every last gallon of Canadian water is measured and allocated to some future Canadian use.
We fear the direction in which we are going. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) has now had water resources taken away from him; he is now responsible for Eskimos and northern affairs. Also, his former parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Turner) is now Minister without Portfolio. They have both been neutralized and are out of the way because they are rather difficult to handle. But I give the Minister without Portfolio credit for an excellent speech made in Washington on this issue. I am sure that in his heart he still feels as keenly as we do on the question of Canada-United States relations with respect to water.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to your attention the present situation with respect to the developments on the Columbia River Treaty projects, the destruction of many thousands of acres of land and forests, the destruction of 50 miles of beaches between Castelgar and Revelstoke, and the depletion of our fishlife and other recreational resources that we have to endure as a result of Liberal policy. During the hearings before the External Affairs Committee we were refused any breakdown as to the estimated cost of the construction of the dams, the clearing of the basins and compensation for the property owners affected. We expect this government to be able to give us a progress report on this development at the appropriate time.

There is a great deal of dissatisfaction with the policy of B.C. Hydro with respect to compensation for properties affected, Mr. Speaker. That is the reason for the Arrow Lakes Property Owners Protective Association being formed, with a membership of over 250. A committee representing these owners has met with Hon. Ray Williston, Minister of Lands and Forests of the province of British Columbia, and explained their problems. I might say that this committee is composed of members of all parties. The chairman is a member of the Social Credit party, the secretary is a member of this party, and members of the executive are members of the Conservative and Liberal parties.
Time does not permit me to deal with this issue at the present time, but I just mention it to indicate some of the problems that are already arising as a result of the developments along the Arrow lakes, regardless of what the External Affairs Committee was told.
I have here an editorial written by the Social Credit candidate for Kaslo-Slocan in the last provincial election. He is the owner and editor of the newspaper. He indicates in this article that water resources minister Ray Williston spent an entire morning with the executive members of the Arrow Lakes Property Owners Protective Association. These people were protesting to him. All they want is justice. As a result of that meeting the Social Credit candidate wrote this editorial. I mention this so the house will understand the situation that exists at this time.
We believe that this problem can only be solved by discussions with the provinces concerned and, second, by keeping the people of Canada fully informed of developments. Let the processes of democracy function. Get the
The Address-Mr. Ricard co-operation of the farmers, their organizations and industry who are interested in a national water policy. Third, let us have a debate in this parliament before a national water policy is established so that everything is aboveboard, so we know what is being done and so the Canadian people will be informed.
This water game is not being played for fun but for our survival. The national water policy we adopt will determine within two or three generations which parts of this continent will keep on growing and developing and which will shrivel for lack of water. Much of our control over Canada's water resources has already been given away.
Single-purpose water resource developments are destroying other natural values at an unprecedented rate. In our rush to develop impoundments for water storage and power generation at the lowest possible cost, we seem to be forgetting the permanence of our present decisions. Tomorrow's values are ignored for today's expediency, and in some cases expediency on the part of governments and individual members of this house.
We are in urgent need of a national policy to guide the use of water within our own country so that our water resources will be developed by Canadians for Canadians of this and future generations.

Mr. Speaker, I should like, at the outset, to congratulate you on your appointment as Speaker of this assembly and to wish you every success.
I should also like to congratulate and offer my best wishes to the member for Humb-er-St. George's (Mr. Batten) and the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) on their respective appointments as Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees, and Deputy Chairman of Committees.
May I also congratulate the mover (Mr. Goyer) and the seconder (Mr. Stanbury) of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne in recognition of their brilliant performance, which is all to the credit of those they represent here in the house.
Before going further in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I thank the people of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot who for the fifth time have done me the honour of sending me here as their representative.
The people of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot must also be congratulated for the way in which

January 31. 1966

The Address-Mr. Ricard they voted; they were not influenced by the campaign of demagogy and smear against my leader, my party and myself.
People of my riding are noted for their good judgment and they refused to be misled by the improper arguments used by my opponents. You can rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that if I am here today it is no thanks to the hon. members opposite, for they bent every effort to try and defeat me.
During the election campaign there was an almost uninterrupted parade of the so-called big guns. First of all, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) came and he was as successful as he has been in all his undertakings since he entered politics; then, the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Pepin), the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who came, in turn, in an effort to enrol the people of the Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot riding. But they preached in the desert and on the night of the election, on November 8 last, your humble servant was once more re-elected with a majority of 3,501 votes.
However do not think for a moment that superhuman efforts were not attempted; a defeat of the member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot, who was considered as the repository of conservatism in the province of Quebec, appeared so desirable, that every possible means were resorted to. Evening dancing parties were organized in my riding, Mr. Speaker, with buffet suppers, and refreshments of the most varied qualities and kinds; luncheon baskets were distributed, oil bills were paid to some people. In short, every possible means was put to use but they proved useless since, as I said before, the people of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot are not to be taken in that way.
I could provide a whole series, a list of addresses whereby one could check all these facts.
There even was a whole network of impersonators; need I say more? Those who might not quite believe this should read the newspaper account of the prosecution of a certain person-as a personal means of protection-by the crown attorney at the suggestion of my opponent's organizers.
To me, the most amusing episode was to hear, on election night, the spontaneous comment of the hon. member for Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance) who, in answer to the question: "What is your greatest disappointment

regarding the results of this November 8 election?" said, without a moment of hesitation "The re-election of the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot".

I see that, in that respect, he had the support of his political colleagues. It is true then-it is even truer than I thought- that they really tried to beat me, but they are the ones who were beaten, not me.
Mr. Speaker, I am here to bring to light the aspirations and the needs of my riding. During two week ends since the reading of the Speech from the Throne, I visited my riding to get information, to inquire about the opinions of my constituents.
I must say that the Speech from the Throne has spread not only disappointment but also resentment among the people, especially among older pepole, who thought that the present government would listen to reason and increase old age pensions.
But no, the "Six Buck Boys" once again proved to the people that they are against paying to our senior citizens the reasonable pension to which they are entitled.
Our rural and urban population, workers as well as farmers, were lamentably disappointed to learn that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, the Liberals' baby, has been carefully maintained. Here again, people thought that the Liberal government would listen to reason and withdraw the 11 per cent tax, giving effect to the suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: COPPER-EXPORTS TO OFF-SHORE DESTINATIONS-CHANGE IN ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to hon. members and I apologize for the interruption. I wish to make a statement respecting the supply of copper for domestic purposes.

I wish to inform the house of a change in the arrangements for control of exports to offshore destinations of copper scrap, copper alloy scrap and copper bearing scrap. It has become necessary to suspend export quotas effective immediately and withhold further export permits in the interest of orderly marketing and Canadian supply. I am pleased to say that the action being taken is the result of a co-operative effort between the scrap dealers, the consumers of scrap and the department.
In recent weeks, the price for primary copper on the London Metal Exchange has reached all-time high levels. The daily "spot'f quotation on the exchange for January 26 was the equivalent of 89.54 cents, Canadian funds. This compares with the Canadian producers' price to domestic consumers at 45 cents, Canadian funds.
Export prices for copper scrap tend to follow movements of the London market price for primary copper. In Canada the influence of these high and rising prices has been reflected in a steadily widening spread between the value of scrap for export and for the domestic market. This spread reached the point where the market became disorganized. Consumers in Canada were unable to obtain their normal requirements of brass mill and refinery grades of scrap copper even though the actual movement of offshore exports under quota restriction has been small in relation to the rate of generation of scrap in Canada.
In suspending quotas and the issuance of export permits in the interest of stabilizing the market at North American levels, I have been concerned to avoid undue hardship for those who have been trading in the expectation of being permitted to export scrap. In this connection, I have received the assurance of major copper scrap consumers that they will offer to purchase, for prompt delivery, at price levels which would prevent such hardship, inventories of copper scrap acquired in the expectation of exporting under the quotas.
I have also their assurances that thereafter, once the market is stabilized, they will continue to take refinery and brass mill grades of scrap copper at prices which are competitive with those offered by United States consumers.
There may be limited quantities of scrap materials of a type not normally consumed by Canadian industry for which export permits will be considered. Exports to the United
January 31, 1966

States of all forms of copper scrap remain free of control.
As a means of continuing the degree of co-operation which has characterized this arrangement, it is intended to form an industry advisory committee to assist in keeping the copper situation under review while the supply emergency in the world market persists.
This committee will be properly representative of the industry and the trade. It would need to embrace spokesmen from the primary producers, the rod mills, the wire mills, the brass mills, the ingot makers and foundries and the trade handling secondary materials.

so far, namely the need to speed up the war on poverty, in all the areas where it is found today in Canada. Other measures are new and tonight I would like to point out a measure which in my opinion, is fundamental, and meets the present needs of Canada; it is the reform in depth of some federal departments, and in particular the creation of a Department of Manpower which goes to the core of the economic programs which we must set up today in Canada.
Before going on to that administrative reform and indicating the two fundamental matters which I feel it is important to mention, I would like to recall in passing two statements found in the Speech from the Throne which seem very significant. I feel that they led to interpretations which do not correspond, I am sure of that, to the spirit of the party which has in fact supported them. Here they are. The first one deals with the need to maintain the fundamental powers of the central government, the federal government.
We believe that to preserve a country which deserves to be protected, a country in which we will be happy to live, it is important to have a strong and efficient central government, and, on the other hand, that bilingualism and biculturalism spread more and more in Canada, not only at the federal level, which is the responsibility of this parliament, but also in provincial fields, other than those of Quebec.
I feel that balance should be maintained between those two fundamentals of our country. On the one hand, the need for strong provincial governments and, in the case of Quebec, the provincial government certainly has a special responsibility, that of being the stronghold of French culture in Canada. On the other hand, federalists who are to be found in all schools of thought, do not want this provincial autonomy to be achieved at the cost of the existence and development of our country as a whole.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In my opinion, this is fair, and we have taken it into consideration in the opting out formula; it is fair to allow the provinces and particularly Quebec to exercise their authority in fields allotted to them by virtue of the
January 31, 1966	COMMONS
constitution. At the same time this tendency must not go so far that the expansion of a province should be detrimental to the country as a whole or detrimental to the development of a culture, the French culture, which cannot be conceived solely in terms of a single province but in terms of the whole country. I am convinced that the government in office at present wishes to maintain the policy it established since it came to power, that is to offer the provinces the opting out formula with regard to the fields allotted to them by virtue of the constitution. At the same time, I think that the Speech from the Throne showed, as stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), that this measure should not be interpreted as an indication that provincial powers are granted to the detriment of the essential powers of our federal state.
Another matter of national urgency is increased help for universities. This is a field that comes under provincial jurisdiction, but as it happens, the central government is pursuing a policy which has already been applied in the past. The Prime Minister has announced recently that grants to universities would be increased from $2 to $5 per capita in each province. In providing such a wide measure of special assistance, the government recognizes the urgency of the situation, as indicated at the end of the report of the economic council of Canada about which I intend to speak. I see two main reasons for the administrative reforms applied in some departments: first, administrative efficiency; I think that all modern states face the dilemma, on the one hand, of efficiency justifying more and more decentralization in public administration and, on the other hand, complex international, national and local problems requiring the administration to become constantly better co-ordinated and more centralized.
How can those two different phenomena be reconciled? Administrative policies should then be sufficiently flexible to permit efficient control and administration, yet broad enough to allow the necessary co-ordination between the various policies.
The establishment of a department of manpower should tend to solve this twofold problem by having one department deal with the essential development services and the manpower essential to the national development of the economy, on the one hand, and a central administration just large enough to exercise efficient control over administrative services, on the other.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay
The same principles seem to warrant the creation of the new department of energy. Activities are spread over several departments and their co-ordination is becoming increasingly more difficult because no practical policies can be worked out as long as sources of energy cannot be substituted for one another. With one single department, such sources of energy, whether it be electricity, coal or atomic energy, can be coordinated in one administrative unit.
It would be advisable that this example given by the government in a few fields be followed in other areas of public administration.
The second reason in favour of the creation of this department of manpower, or reorganization of others, is the necessity of meeting important needs at present within our community. The creation of a new department shows that the government recognizes the existence of important problems and the need for new and efficient policies.
No one will deny, especially after the magnificent report just submitted by the economic council, that one of the basic problems of Canada today is that of manpower. That fact is brilliantly illustrated in the report and I want to congratulate the chairman, Dr. Deutsch, and all the senior officials of the economic council who have rendered a great service not only to the house and to the government but to the whole population of Canada by analysing the present economic needs and by showing exactly to the public the necessity for basic reforms at various indicated levels. Every page of the report bears witness to the importance attached by the council to a labour force adapted to current economic problems. The consequence of inadequate manpower is depressed incomes. That incomes are too low is obvious when one makes comparison with the United States and also between various parts of Canada.
This is seen when one economic sector is compared to another. Insufficient income, a slower growth rate, disparities in economic structures, we find a manpower that is not adjusted, not prepared to today's economic tasks.
The establishment of a department of manpower is therefore a first response. I think we will have to have more and more important measures in this field. I think it is a first response, in the mind of the government, to this need pointed out in the report of the economic council.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay
In the field of energy and resources, I simply point out the immense work carried out by the Canadian resources council in the last few years, precisely to make the Canadian population and government conscious of the necessity of an energy and resources policy well adjusted to present problems. It is a problem in which the provinces have large responsibilities. It comes under the jurisdiction of the central government because these energy resources go from one province to another, even from one country to another and because the central government has a very important role to play particularly in the matter of co-ordination.
This department of energy will be, in my opinion, the nucleus that will allow us a more efficient approach to the problems arising in that field.
I want to point out that those administrative reforms answer the present needs of our society.
I also want to mention the establishment of a new department, the department of the solicitor general, which will be responsible from now on for organizing the whole police force and for helping in the war which the government intends to wage against organized crime. I do want to praise the government very sincerely for entering this field with determination.
I remember how, a few weeks only after I was appointed minister of citizenship and immigration, police authorities advised me of the alarming situation in Canada and even in the United States with regard to the infiltration of subversive forces in our society. At that time, I agreed, as minister of immigration-and I am happy to see the present minister is following and even developing that policy-to set up a special division responsible for co-operating with police authorities in tracking down those elements which continued, by all possible means, to defy law and order in Canada. That co-operation paid off in the high number of deportations of people considered as undesirable in our country.

Doubtless we will need, in the field of Indian affairs, a democratic policy which has already been initiated some time ago. Mr. Speaker, the fact that this debate is drawing to a close is not going to prevent me from being repetitious in extending to you, individually, and to our Speaker, that first commoner of this house, my congratulations upon your appointments. I join with the concerted unanimity of opinion as to your ability, which in itself indicates that there is on all sides of this house the intention to co-operate with you in your judgments, and in your control of the activities of this house.
I should like also to extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, because when I came here first in 1949 I had that very great privilege, and then very terrible task; so I am somewhat of an authority. I want to tell those two hon. members that it has been a long time since we have heard their equal in this house.
I enter this debate tonight because I want to deal with a problem of concern to me and, at the same time, as evidenced by the speeches of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) and Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), to other western members. This subject has reference to the administration of our national parks.
January 31. 1966



At the outset I should like to say there is today no greater national asset in this country than our national parks. Those parks today are extremely popular and are being visited by millions of Canadians, as well as others. One of our problems relates to the citizens who live in one or two of our national parks, and the relationship of this situation to the fact that several other provinces are considering the establishment of more national parks.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson at page 109 of Hansard said:
We are not complaining about the national parks policy as enunciated.
I am not quite certain what the hon. member for Edmonton West is not complaining about. The hon. member for Jasper-Edson stated:
We are not complaining about the national parks policy as enunciated. We are complaining about the administration and the disregard of the rights of Canadian citizens who live in two part townships, one being Jasper and the other being Banff.
I think that is a fair enough statement, and I think that justice should be done in respect of any minority in Canada, even though it be a minority of one. I think justice has a responsibility to be all pervading, and the majority is entitled to justice too.
Perhaps I should suggest that a portion of our trouble in respect of parks administration relates to the time when parks were first established. In this regard I am reminded of the comments made by the first prime minister of Canada in 1887, 78 years ago. In a debate in this House of Commons Sir John A. Macdonald said:
We can sell or lease. I have the strong inclination to lease so that we can retain absolute control over the character of our parks.
Sir Richard Cartwright, of the opposition, said:
I think a limit ought to be fixed for these leases.
Sir John A. replied:
Twenty one years are suggested as sufficient, but people will not build handsome houses on a 21 year lease. If there is to be a limit at all there must be the right of renewal. I think the hon. gentleman and the house may trust any government with the settlement of that question in the interest of the property.
When he spoke of the interest of the property no doubt Sir John was referring to the governmental retained absolute control over the character of parks.
When Sir John answered Sir Richard, there was no difficulty envisaged such as we are
The Address-Mr. Laing faced with today. We have arrived at the point today where park business is big business. Our annual budget in respect of parks amounts to approximately $23 million, yet our annual total receipts are in the neighbourhood of only $3 million. I do not think anyone suggests that we should try to balance our receipts and disbursements in respect of parks.
Our difficulties and problems arise from an attempt to retain by restrictive and protectionist control the conditions and traffic in our parks. Surely it is the opinion at this time of the department responsible, as well as those who have obtained leases in parks, that the maintenance and efficiency of operation is of uppermost importance. We have had difficulties with leaseholders, and I shall not identify them. Perhaps I should give this house one or two examples. The first example involved three leasehold lots on which the department received a total of $45 annually. The leases were assigned for a consideration of $141,000. The second case involves a lot upon which we received $30 per year rent. This lease was assigned for a consideration of $1200 per year; the sublessee undertook to invest $30,000 in a building, the whole property to return to the assignor after 18 years.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
So on September 18, 1964, I made a pronouncement in respect of park policy in the house and the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) said that he agreed with the policy. Well, I hope he has read it, because I said this, among other things:
A change in policy toward residence in national parks has long been required...
For this reason, we have adopted a policy that will eventually exclude private residential occupation of park land unless it is required by persons who provide services to the park and its visitors. No new uses of park land for summer homes, cottages, or permanent residence will be allowed unless it ^ is clear that the permanent or temporary resident is providing some essential service to park visitors, or engaged in the administration, operation and protection of the national parks. Such improper occupation of park land by individuals as now exists will be eliminated gradually.
This was part of the policy, because we are coming to the point where we have a small number of Canadians enjoying permanent residence in the parks that is denied to all other Canadians, and we speak of justice. I am quite certain that the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, and probably the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), are thinking in terms of private enterprise. I want to make it as emphatic as I can that
482	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Laing we are dealing here with a national trust, and because it is a national trust some, but not all, of the ordinary principles of private enterprise can prevail.
We have to ensure that we maintain the parks for the purposes for which they were set up, namely the enjoyment and the recreation of the Canadian people. We have an amazing increase in attendance at our parks.
I could give the house some very interesting figures, but I do not want to bother hon. members with these at the moment. However, at the present time we have increases that are nothing short of spectacular. The most spectacular of all was at Terra Nova park, in our newest province of Newfoundland, where attendance in the parks last year was 62 per cent over the previous year; and we are running at a rate of increase of 8 per cent, 10 per cent and 12 per cent in other parks.
In the fiscal year 1962-63 we had 7,426,000 visitors to the parks. In the nine months ending December 31 last we had 9,349,000 visitors. Since I came to office we have added some 7,000 separate camping sites in the parks, and we find in our western parks that people are lined up for 24 hours waiting to get into them-that is, waiting for someone to move out.
Therefore I am quite certain that we have to take the action that is necessary to service the increase and maintain the purposes for which the parks were set out. We will see to it that no injustice is done to those who are resident in the parks. We have said that if their tasks require their constant presence in the parks, then no change whatsoever will be made. At the present time all we have done is say to those who want to assign leases that we will not assign the lease as it stands, but they will turn over the lease and we will give them a 42-year terminal lease.
With regard to leases that are in vogue on that basis at the present time, if they have 17 or 18 years to run, when the 17 or 18 years is terminated they will get a full 42-year lease thereafter. We have undertaken at the end of that 42-year period to pay compensation for the residual value that the lessee has in the property. I think nothing can be fairer than that. I have had my department make a review of what is the practice in other provinces and other states in their parks and what they are doing there, and without question ours is the most generous lessee condition that we have been able to find anywhere.
In the province of British Columbia the term of lease is 21 years. In the province of

Alberta concessions and permits are granted up to five years. In Saskatchewan leases at commercial sites are granted for 10 years. In Manitoba leases at commercial sites are granted for 21 years. In Ontario they are granted for 21 years, and very, very few of them have been granted. In the United States they are granted up to a maximum of 30 years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I raised a question on the orders of the day concerning the reported expenditure by the Royal Canadian Air Force of $20 million for the purchase of eight French jet aircraft which, according to the press, are to be used for the transport of cabinet ministers and VIP's. My point in raising this question was that if these planes are to be used mainly for this purpose the people of Canada will surely question the need for the expenditure of such a large amount of money.
The expenditure of $10 million on these planes would mean approximately 50 cents for every man, woman and child in the country. If the planes are to be bought for some other purpose in addition to the transport of cabinet ministers and VIP's I think it would be well to clarify the situation so as to present a proper picture to the people of this country. Otherwise, as I suggested, the spending of $10 million for the transport of cabinet ministers and VIP's would surely result in a
January 31, 1966	COMMONS
further diminution of the present government's position in the public esteem, something which it would almost certainly wish to avoid.
I asked the Minister of National Defence this morning to make a statement clarifying the situation. At that time Mr. Speaker ruled it was a question which might be better placed on the order paper. However, feeling the matter was more urgent and that it would be well to clarify it more quickly than can usually be done when we wait for answers to questions placed on the order paper, I decided to raise it this evening in the hope that the minister or someone speaking for him would tell us the real story about these planes and their purchase.

speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity to debate the issue of farm machinery prices. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is interested in this matter because he indicated when he was out in the west that farm machinery prices were away out of proportion to the price the farmer receives for his products.
It is no secret that one reason so many farmers are forced out of the farming industry is the high cost of farm machinery, and other services of which they must avail themselves. I base my argument on personal experience and on statistics from the dominion bureau of statistics tables which I hold in my hand.

For instance, according to the selected index numbers of prices of commodities and services used by farmers, based on 1935-39 equalling 100, farm machinery in 1949 stood at 158.3. But during the 15 years to 1964 it rose to 279.6. The composite index excluding cost of living expenses rose during the same period from 204.1 to 308.6-a tremendous rise in the cost which farmers had to pay for farm machinery.
Index numbers of wholesale prices of Canadian farm products based on 1935-39 equalling 100 are as follows: In 1949, the index for all farm products stood at 228.7. In 1964 it dropped 10 points to 218.3. For field products it stood in 1949 at 191.9, dropping 22 points to 169.4, in 1964. For animal products it stood at 265.4 in 1949 rising only 2 points to 267.2 in 1964.
Using the same basic index figure we find that in 1949 the index number for wheat, oats and barley was 255.4. In 1964-15 years later-it stood at only 258, a mere 3 point increase. It is no wonder that the machinery companies have made such a tremendous profit.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I only have the statistics for the last ten years, from 1954 to 1964. Value of farm implement and equipment sales rose from $146 million in 1954 to $366 million in 1964, a tremendous increase. What a sad story this is.
I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to these statistics. They tell the real story of why farmers must leave their farms and seek employment in some other industry. It is my hope that the Minister of Agriculture will study these statistics which I have been able to present to him, so that he can base his decision on these figures which tell the story of the dilemma in which farmers all across Canada find themselves at present.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on orders of the day this morning I addressed two questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) expressing the hope that at an early date the government might make a statement as to its position with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway, in the light of certain developments that are taking place in this country.
Everyone in Canada is aware of the fact that the C.P.R. is reneging on some of its obligations. Across the west in particular

there is a hue and cry concerning the dropping of certain railway services. The dropping of the Dominion is a case in point, and there are others.
Not only is the C.P.R. cutting back on its service to the people of this country but some of us think this is in violation of the agreements entered into by that railway in the last century. Certainly it shows a lack of appreciation of the tremendous grants made to that company. In addition we feel the C.P.R. is reneging on its obligations to its employees.
References have been made a number of times this session to the lay-offs of employees that are taking place. In addition to that I should like to mention just briefly that in 1965 this parliament passed what, in my view, are two very valuable pieces of legislation, the Canada Pension Plan and the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. I draw attention to the fact that the C.P.R. is flouting the intent as well as the provisions of both of these pieces of legislation. It is denying to its employees consultation with regard to the effect of the Canada Pension Plan on their private pension rights, and it is also denying the benefits which that plan was intended to provide. Likewise, with respect to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code it is quarreling over every little detail it possibly can. This can only lead to a very serious situation on the C.P.R., and I feel that parliament cannot sit idly by while this sort of thing goes on.
I do not pretend to be a prophet or the son of a prophet, but I see certain things as almost sure to happen in this country if a firm stand is not taken. The Canadian Pacific Railway, because it wants to get out of the passenger service business on its railway lines, has taken this attitude. On the other hand, that same organization, with respect to its Canadian Pacific Airlines, is endeavouring to get more air routes and more opportunities to make money in that field of transportation.
What bothers some of us is that the government of the day seems to be condoning both of these approaches by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is reneging as far as its obligations with regard to railway passenger service is concerned, yet is trying to get more profits from passenger service in the air.
I am concerned about the attitude of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who, instead of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), is here to answer the question, because of his
January 31, 1966	COMMONS
announcement last July concerning the appointment of Mr. Wheatcroft, who was assigned the task of investigating air line services in this country.
When I read the terms of reference under which Mr. Wheatcroft was appointed I saw the possibility of a report coming down, with the suggestion that it might be wise to increase the competition on main lines in this country. Surely this is not the kind of reward to be given to the Canadian Pacific Railway for having welshed on its responsibility in railway services. Surely this company should not be given greater opportunities in air transportation.
It is my feeling that we should have a clear statement with respect to government intention regarding transportation, and I support the view in this country today that the time has come to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway. I hope we will not be faced with the situation at the time of take-over under which the government will merely take over its unprofitable operations, and that is a situation which could develop. This company may discontimue its passenger services. This country will of necessity need a continuation of these services. This will require a shift of responsibility in which the government will be involved, and a necessity to provide some sort of an establishment to maintain these passenger services.
When the time comes for the government to take over the Canadian Pacific operation it must take it over in its entirety. This will have to be done, not just with respect to the uneconomical or unprofitable operations, but with respect to all its operations.
There are some who will condone the taking over by the government of the unprofitable operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I believe, as do my colleagues, that we should be concerned as to whether or not we have a right in this country to expect and obtain from the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway that service which is necessary. On the other hand I am concerned that the government not condone the direction of operations which this company is inclined to adopt.
When we take over the Canadian Pacific Railway we can well afford to pay for its properties at their fair market value, less the value of the land and money grants made to this company.

speechtext:
I should also recall to hon. members that, I believe in 1903, a very salutary provision was put on the statute books when the original board of railway commissioners was established, and I think it would be quite impossible to enforce these obligations if they were not enforceable in a proper kind of court, such as the Board of Transport Commissioners is, with the proper kind of appeal on questions of law to the supreme court, and with the appeal that exists under the present law to the privy council on questions of fact.
I,	and any other member of the government, would be under some limitation, I think, in making a premature reply about the particular question of the Dominion, because we must surely consider the case ourselves before pre-judging it. Well, indeed we should not pre-judge it; we should make a judgment only after hearing both sides of the case.
January 31. 1966

speechtext:
It applies to any matter on which the Board of Transport Commissioners has made an adjudication. I must say I was rather attracted by something like the suggestion made today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I think I should like to get a little advice about it, but it did seem to me there might be a great deal to be said, if it could be arranged without the members of the government in any way prejudging any question. I refer to the setting up of the house committee on transportation, or a joint committee of both houses and having the railways come before them and other parties who are interested, not just in this narrow question of the Dominion-though it is
important enough-but in the whole question of the future of passenger service on the railways, and letting everyone who would like to be heard, be heard on this matter, and be heard before we go on with the railway legislation that the government has in contemplation.
